rows.title: Null/unknown narrowing rule is unspecified: three documents resolve an ordering-on-nullable predicate at three different points

anchors.quote: - Forbids any predicate that applies `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=` to an operand that can be `null` — lint must reject it,
set") must explicitly guard with an equality/`!= null` check first; the grammar gives no shorthand for "ordering that
THEN load fails unless the row's predicate handles `unknown` explicitly (equality only), so `unknown` is never ordered
a `require` row whose predicate cannot be evaluated over a `null` yields `Unsatisfiable(kind, failed_predicates)`

rows.statement: ADR-0069's Forbids block rejects at lint time any ordering on an operand that CAN be null, yet its Negative clause tells authors to guard with `!= null` first; AC-069 makes load succeed when the predicate 'handles unknown explicitly (equality only)'; RUNBOOK 4a.3 describes a runtime Unsatisfiable path for a predicate that cannot be evaluated over null. No document states how the lint decides a guard is present (which conjunct shapes, `or` branches, `not`, nesting), so the same predicate is a lint error, a lint pass, or a runtime gate depending on which text the implementer reads.
rows.why_before_step5: Does not touch Step 5 (rk-types) but blocks the lint / rk-select workstream (Step 7b, AC-069, AC-079, AC-520): two implementers produce different load-time outcomes for every ordinal-facet predicate, and since all four ordinals carry `unknown` in facets.toml that is most of the catalog's require rows.
rows.remediation: A superseding or amending ADR (never an edit to 0069) that states the narrowing rule as a syntactic pattern the lint recognises (e.g. `x != null and <ordering on x>` at the same conjunction level, no `or`, no `not`), and says explicitly whether the RUNBOOK 4a.3 runtime Unsatisfiable path exists at all or is unreachable by construction; amend AC-069's Verified-by to name that pattern.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. The narrowing gap is real: ADR-0069:62 tells authors to guard with `!= null`, :66 forbids ordering on any operand that CAN be null, AC-069:1017 says 'equality only', and the P9 lint (lint.py:328) rejects every ordering next to a `?` ref, guard or not. But 'three documents, three points' is overstated: RUNBOOK:1510 is the AC-079 runtime half, which AC-079:1045 records as split from the lint. The real nearby defect: RUNBOOK:1510 names the outcome `Unsatisfiable` (AC-054's step-4 gate) while AC-079:1036 routes at step 2 as `gate_opened { reason: unknown_facet }`.
rows.material_reason: NEW: known-issues rows for ADR-0069 are limited to ADR-0032-MARK-46 (refinement lineage); no row records the guard question or the RUNBOOK/AC-079 reason mismatch. Priority P1 is wrong on its own premise: AC-069 and AC-079 are P1-blocked and excluded from Step 7b's acceptance set (RUNBOOK:2006 'minus the P1-blocked rows AC-069, AC-070, AC-072, AC-076, AC-079'), and ADR-0069 is cited by no other criterion (register :6491). No Phase-1 workstream is blocked; P2 (record contradiction, resolved before the blocked rows re-enter).
rows.corrected_statement: No text states whether an equality/`!= null` guard narrows an operand for ADR-0069's lint: the ADR's Negative clause (:62) presumes it does, its Decision/Forbids (:66), AC-069's 'equality only' (:1017) and the P9 lint's regex (lint.py:328) presume it does not. Separately, RUNBOOK 4a.3 (:1510) names the null-at-runtime outcome `Unsatisfiable(kind, failed_predicates)` — AC-054's step-4 gate — while AC-079 (:1036), which the same paragraph invokes, routes at step 2 as `gate_opened { reason: unknown_facet, axis }`. The catalog carries 198 ordering comparisons on the four unknown-capable ordinals and no guards [measured].

rows.title: 'Quantifiers over null are vacuously true' inverts `any`, and the design restates it over an empty set instead of null

anchors.quote: "Absent `?` inputs are `null`; quantifiers over `null` are vacuously true; `null == null`; any other operation on `null` is a lint error."
absent optional inputs are `null` and quantifiers over an empty set are vacuously true (**ADR-0032**)
`checks = ["evidence.any(GreenAt)", "evidence.none(Findings.items[evidence in {Reproduced, MutationSurvived}])"]`
| **6** | **Absence of evidence is a block, and the absence is usually silent.** `Result<Findings, StepError>`. *Forbids:* an absent digest read as `pass`;

rows.statement: ADR-0032 fixes one rule for `none/all/any`; in standard semantics `any` over nothing is false, so a literal implementation makes `evidence.any(GreenAt)` succeed when evidence is absent. The authoritative design restates the rule as 'over an empty set' (a present, empty list), which is a different object from an absent `?` ref and which, read with design principle 6 ('absence of evidence is a block'), makes an empty evidence collection satisfy both the `any` and `none` stage-exit checks in the schema's own example. Only AC-434 cites ADR-0032 and it tests display of `unknown`, not null semantics, so no criterion pins either reading.
rows.why_before_step5: Not a Step-5 item, but the predicate evaluator (Step 7b) built from either text passes a stage-exit check on zero evidence, the exact failure the design's principle 6 and ADR-0080 exist to prevent. Two implementers diverge on `any`, and on whether an empty list is treated like null.
rows.remediation: Supersede/amend ADR-0032 with per-quantifier semantics (`all`/`none` over null or empty = true; `any` = false) and state explicitly whether an empty present list and an absent ref share semantics; add an AC with a must-fail fixture (`any` over absent evidence must not pass). Correct design line 541 to match.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. ADR-0032:35 and schema :231 fix one rule for all three quantifiers; a literal `any` over null = true inverts standard semantics, and design :541 restates it 'over an empty set' — a present, empty object — with nothing distinguishing the two. The only `any` in the live set is the schema's stage-exit example (:57), whose `evidence` list is never null but can be empty [measured: catalog uses `none` 47x, `all` 2x, `any` 0x]. Register :6468 confirms AC-434 is ADR-0032's sole citer. The drift is real although the design disclaims grammar ownership (:1967).
rows.material_reason: NEW: no known-issues row (searched 'vacuous', 'adr-0032', 'empty set'); ARCH-10.x-L-001 records only that the design does not restate the grammar. P1 is inflated: the only divergent form (`any`) has zero uses in the catalog and one in a schema example; `none`/`all` over null or empty are true under both the ADR and standard semantics, so two implementers agree on every predicate the Phase-1 catalog loads. P2 — a record contradiction with a latent, not live, build consequence.

rows.title: No precedence or associativity for `and`/`or`/`not`; ADR-0048 declines to define one and mixed unparenthesised forms are undefined
rows.known_issue_match: none (F33-LIM-013 recorded only that parentheses were missing)

anchors.quote: grouping is needed for readable `and`/`or` compositions without inventing precedence rules by convention.
operators `== != < <= > >= in`; boolean connectives `and or not`; literals are string/number/bool/`null`. No user functions.

rows.statement: Across ADR-0033/0048/0049/0070 and schema 9a.3/9b.18 no precedence, associativity or binding strength is given for `not`, `and`, `or`, comparison and `in` [measured: 'precedence' occurs in no grammar ADR]. ADR-0048 adds parentheses 'without inventing precedence rules', but does not say that an unparenthesised `a and b or c` is a lint error, so a parser must either invent precedence or reject; ADR-0070 replaced the regex with a parser and the P9 lint's behaviour is the only de facto answer.
rows.why_before_step5: Parser is a Step-7b deliverable; a grammar with no precedence cannot be implemented identically twice. Not P1 because a lint-error-on-mixed-connectives choice is cheap and reversible.
rows.remediation: One amending ADR fixing precedence (`not` > comparison/`in` > `and` > `or`, left-associative) or declaring mixed unparenthesised connectives a lint error; state the quote character set and escaping for string literals in the same record.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. No precedence, associativity or 'mixed unparenthesised is an error' rule exists in ADR-0033/0048/0049/0070 or schema 9a.3 [measured: precedence/associativ/binds tighter match only ADR-0048:21]. The bracketed claim "'precedence' occurs in no grammar ADR" is literally false — it occurs at the finder's own anchor ADR-0048:21 — but the intended claim holds. The P9 lint is a vocabulary checker, not a parser (lint.py:327-340), so no de facto answer exists. The catalog has 0 unparenthesised mixed connectives [measured].
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN, not NEW: F33-LIM-013 (spikes/F33-DRAFT.md:62) records parentheses as a grammar gap and AC-15.3-P-003 (acceptance-criteria.md:6526) records that the seventeen grammar ADRs including 0048/0049/0070 'have not been audited'. The specific absence of a precedence rule is not recorded, so the sharpening stands. P2 is sound: the parser must choose, but the catalog gives it nothing to disagree about, so no workstream is blocked.
rows.corrected_statement: No precedence or associativity is defined for `not`/`and`/`or`/comparison/`in` in any grammar record; ADR-0048:21 mentions 'precedence' only to say parentheses avoid inventing one, and neither it nor any later record declares an unparenthesised mixed form legal or illegal. The P9 lint does not parse connectives, so no reference behaviour exists. The v0 catalog contains no unparenthesised mixed form.

rows.title: No rule distinguishes a bare value literal from a field or root reference inside a predicate

anchors.quote: roots are step inputs, facets, `rigor`, `item`; `.field` access; `len()`; `none/all/any(<field> in […])` with the element's fields in scope
Quantifier bodies take full comparisons: `all(owner != null and due != null)`, not membership only.

rows.statement: `rigor >= recommended` and `kind == bug` use bare identifiers as value literals; `owner != null` uses a bare identifier as a field of the element in scope. Nothing says how the parser tells `bug` (literal) from `owner` (field): whether the RHS of a comparison is always a literal, whether field-to-field comparison is expressible, or how a facet value that coincides with a field name is read. ADR-0033 also writes the quantifier without a receiver while every example is `<list>.none(...)`.
rows.why_before_step5: Parser correctness at Step 7b; two implementers disambiguate differently and both pass the P9 catalog by accident.
rows.remediation: Amending ADR: state 'an unquoted identifier in value position (RHS of a comparison or member of an `in` list) is a value literal; a field or root is only ever in operand position; field-to-field comparison requires `${...}` refs', and state the quantifier as `<list-expr>.quant(<body>)`.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. No record states the literal-vs-field rule, and ADR-0033:35 does write the quantifier without a receiver while every example has one. But a de facto rule exists in the corpus: AC-065:892-898 requires a predicate to resolve to 'a registered facet value' or typed verdict, and the P9 lint (lint.py:338-340) accepts a bare identifier only if it is a builtin, a local input, a facet name or a registered bare facet value. facets.toml has no facet-name/facet-value collision [measured], so the vocabulary rule is total today.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN of F33-LIM-014 and AC-15.3-P-003 (unaudited grammar ADRs), as classified. P2 is inflated: AC-065 plus the P9 lint give the implementer a working rule and the registry has no collision, so two implementers do not diverge on any loadable predicate. P3 — the rule should be written down, nothing waits on it.
rows.corrected_statement: No grammar record states how a bare identifier in value position is distinguished from a field; the corpus resolves it by vocabulary (AC-065's 'registered facet value' clause and lint.py:338-340's registry lookup), which is total only while facet names and facet values remain disjoint — they are at this pin. ADR-0033:35's receiver-less `none/all/any(<field> in […])` differs from every worked example, which uses `<list>.quant(...)`.

rows.title: Memo key component count is fixed at five by AC-014/AC-019 while ADR-0021, AC-017 and the schema's step key require at least seven

anchors.quote: GIVEN the memo key `hash(activity id, resolved inputs, card digest, injected KB atoms, toolchain version)`
THEN a `memo_hit` event carrying the key and its five components is appended; a skip is never silent.
THEN it does not hit iteration 1's memo entry, because the loop iteration counter is part of the step key.
- **Step key** = `hash(activity id@version, variant-relevant rigor, step id, resolved input digests, card digest (agent) or toolchain version + command (tool), injected KB atoms)`.

rows.statement: AC-014's property test is 'parameterised over each key component (five cases)' and AC-019's event-schema test asserts a five-component field set, but AC-017 (same area, same ADR) puts the loop iteration counter in the key and the schema's step key adds rigor, step id and the tool command. A key with exactly AC-014's five components collides for two tool steps in one activity with the same inputs and toolchain but different commands, and AC-019's field set cannot carry the iteration counter AC-017 requires.
rows.why_before_step5: rk-kernel::memo is Step 7b; the two instruments (AC-014's five cases, AC-019's field set) cannot both pass against a key that satisfies AC-017. An implementer must pick one and silently fail the other.
rows.remediation: Amend AC-014 and AC-019 to name the per-step component list (activity id@version, rigor variant, step id, resolved input digests, card digest or toolchain version+command, resolved KB atoms, iteration counter) and make the property test 'one case per component'; the design 3.5 row should say the activity-level key and the step key are different formulas.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. Two formulas coexist: the five-component activity key (proposal 4.2, design :322, AC-014:330) and the schema's seven-component step key (:87) plus ADR-0021's iteration counter (:34, AC-017:358). ADR-0021:34 applies the 4.2 key 'per step' while ADR-0043:17 quotes the schema's different formula; AC-016:345 makes the activity key a separate hash. AC-019:374 attaches 'five components' to a step-level `memo_hit`, which cannot carry step id, command or iteration in five fields. The collision case follows from the five-component formula applied per step.
rows.material_reason: NEW: known-issues records only the iteration-counter piece (ADR-0021-FORB-44, F33-LIM-018) and that ADR-0086 keys 'per 0021's step key' (AC-15.3-013); no row records the five-vs-seven mismatch or AC-019's field count. P1 is inflated: AC-014's five miss-cases all pass against a wider key (each named component still changes it), so only AC-019's 'five components' wording is unsatisfiable, and the implementer writes that schema test. Nothing in rk-kernel::memo is blocked; P2 record contradiction.

rows.title: `on_false = "continue"`/`"fail"`: admitted by ADR-0031, forbidden by ADR-0044's scalar rule, used 30 times in the v0 catalog
rows.known_issue_match: none (ADR-0044-FORB-42 records the forbid, not the collision with 0031 or the catalog)

anchors.quote: `on_false ∈ { <earlier-declared step>, continue, fail }` — loop-back only.
"`on_false = { to = "<earlier step>", max = N }`; the scalar form is an error."
"""§9b.14: on_false = { to, max } | 'continue' | 'fail'. Returns (to, max, form_ok)."""

rows.statement: Neither ADR-0044 nor ADR-0046 mentions `continue` or `fail`; 0044 also says a table missing `max` is illegal, so the terminal forms have no legal spelling under a literal reading, and `{ to = "deviate" }` (ADR-0046) has no stated `max` rule either. The P9 lint resolved this by keeping scalar `continue`/`fail` and exempting `deviate` from `max`; the v0 catalog carries 15 `on_false = "fail"` and 15 `on_false = "continue"` [measured, spikes/p9 toml]. A Rust lint written from the accepted ADRs rejects those 30 steps.
rows.why_before_step5: Lint and catalog loader are Step 7b; the shipped catalog and the accepted ADR text disagree, and only the spike script records the resolution.
rows.remediation: Amending ADR stating the closed `on_false` form set: `{ to = <earlier step>, max = N }` | `"continue"` | `"fail"` | `{ to = "deviate", ... }` with `max` required only for loop-back; cite lint.py's on_false_of as the reference behaviour.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured], but the central claim misreads ADR-0044: its Forbids block (:43) is 'Forbids the scalar `on_false = "<step>"` form outright' and its rejected option (:26) is 'bare step-id target'; schema :250 gives the same rationale ('rule 1 demanded a finite max'), which cannot apply to `continue`/`fail`. Catalog count is 15 `continue` + 13 `fail` = 28, not 30 [measured]. Survives: no accepted record states the closed `on_false` form set, and ADR-0044:44 ('a table missing `max` remains as illegal') collides with ADR-0046's `{ to = "deviate" }`, which has no `max` rule.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN, not NEW: AC-15.3-P-003 (acceptance-criteria.md:6526) records ADR-0031 and ADR-0044 among the unaudited grammar records; ADR-0044-FORB-42/44 record the forbids. The deviate/max collision and the absence of a closed form set are not recorded. P2 is inflated once the Forbids block is read: a lint built from the accepted text does not reject the 28 steps. P3 — the closed form set should be written once; the deviate/max gap has no catalog instance.
rows.corrected_statement: ADR-0044's Forbids block scopes the scalar ban to `on_false = "<step>"`, so `continue`/`fail` (ADR-0031:35, 28 catalog uses: 15 `continue`, 13 `fail`) are not forbidden by it. The residual gap is that no accepted record states the closed `on_false` form set, and ADR-0044:44's 'a table missing `max` remains as illegal' contradicts ADR-0046's `on_false.to = "deviate"` table, for which no `max` rule exists; only spikes/p9/lint.py:92 resolves both.

rows.title: `tree_hash` computation for a dirty worktree is unstated although AC-245 demands it with a dirty-worktree property test

anchors.quote: THEN the recorded `tree_hash` is the hash of that same tree object, not of HEAD's commit, not of the index at a later
#### 6.3.2 The record — `(token, tree_hash, deadline)`

rows.statement: ADR-0017, design 6.3.2 and AC-244..250 pin token scope, void and deadline well, but a dirty worktree has no tree object until one is written; no document says whether the hash is `write-tree` over a temporary index, whether untracked or ignored files enter it, or whether `HEAD^{tree}` is used when the tree is clean [measured: 'write-tree', 'untracked' and 'temporary index' occur in no gate text]. AC-249's void rule compares against 'the item's current tree hash' with the same silence, so two implementers void different answers.
rows.why_before_step5: rk-git / gate workstream (Steps 6-7). The void rule is reachable at roughly 1 gate in 14 (F19), so the choice is user-visible.
rows.remediation: One paragraph in design 6.3.2 (and AC-245's Verified-by) naming the algorithm: temporary index from worktree state including untracked-but-not-ignored files, `git write-tree`, same procedure at open and at answer.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. AC-245 (:3150-3157) defines the hash relationally ('that same tree object', not HEAD's commit, not a later index) and demands 'a property test over dirty-worktree fixtures', yet no document says how a tree object is built from a dirty worktree — write-tree/untracked/temporary index occur nowhere in ADR-0017, design 6.3 or AC-244..250 [measured]. ADR-0017:17 says 'the tree at HEAD' while AC-249's fixture 'commits between open and answer', so HEAD^{tree} versus a worktree-derived tree is open. F19 measures drift on commit trailers, not tree hashes.
rows.material_reason: NEW: known-issues rows for ADR-0017/AC-245/AC-249 (ARCH-0.1-023, ARCH-6.6-001/002, ADR-0017-NEG-45, SM-NOBASE-042) record the binding's strength and cost, never the hashing procedure; not in the anomaly pool. rows.statement: Live set: 1 capitalised MUST (a shell comment), 510 lowercase 'must', 90 'must not', 81 'should', 281 'may', 134 'may not', 7 'shall'; no RFC 2119 / key-word declaration exists [measured]. Of the 134 'may not', 123 are prohibitions (mostly ADR Forbids blocks), 10 are epistemic ('fixture may not exist', 'adversary may not have run'), and design 682 is readable both ways. rows.remediation: One sentence in ADR-0085's successor or the ADR README: 'must/may not = obligation/prohibition; should = recommendation; may = permission; epistemic uncertainty is written might'.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim; counts reproduced within file-set tolerance — MUST 1, 'must not' 90, should 81, 'may not' 134, shall 7, no RFC 2119/BCP 14 declaration anywhere [measured]. The claimed ambiguous example is not: design :682 'what a partial tier-2 loss may and may not change' is a permission statement in context (the tier-2 contract it points to), not epistemic. The convention gap exists; the evidence that it ever misleads is weaker than stated.
rows.material_reason: NEW but immaterial: the finder itself records 'every prohibition checked is disambiguated by context' and 'reported as a result, not a blocker'. ADR-0085 already fixes the phrasing that matters for build (EARS/GWT in criteria), and no build or record consequence was shown. P3 with no remediation value beyond a one-line convention note; recorded here as coverage, not as a finding.
rows.corrected_statement: The live set uses lowercase modals throughout (1 capitalised MUST, in a shell comment) with no key-word declaration; 'may not' carries prohibition in ADR Forbids blocks and possibility in a handful of epistemic uses. rows.title: ADR-0021 vs ADR-0059: opposite `memo = false` rules; partial supersession is prose-only, missing from frontmatter and README count

rows.statement: ADR-0021 (D21) and ADR-0043 (SCHEMA-13) are the same decision in two homes — exactly the 0020/0023 shape the README declares — but only 0043 carries the partial supersession by 0059. 0021's forbids block still requires `memo = false` on live-state tool steps while 0059's forbids block makes that per-step declaration illegal; the conflict is acknowledged only in 0021's Evidence prose, with `superseded_by: []`, no `supersedes` entry on 0059, and the README counting nine links where the rule applied to 0043 would give ten.

rows.truth_reason: [measured] All six anchors verbatim. 0021:46 forbids block requires `memo = false`; 0059:61 forbids block makes the per-step declaration illegal. 0021:52 prose says the clause 'is later partially superseded by amendment 29 (ADR 0059)' yet 0021:9 has `superseded_by: []`, 0059:8 supersedes only 0043, and 0021:10 lists 0059 as `related`. rows.material_reason: [measured] known-issues rows ADR-0021-FORB-45 (references/adr/0021-loop-aware-memo-key.md:46) and ADR-0059-NEG-54 (0059:55) record the clause and its withdrawal; no row records the missing frontmatter link, the `related` misuse, or the README nine-link count. rows.statement: Two accepted records dated 2026-09-08 decide the same thing from the same source (evidence-augmentation §4 rec 13): 0074 clause 7 adds the arm as a decided fixture-family property; 0088 adds the same arm and additionally declares it an unrun, must-be-sized spike. 0088's body contains no reference to 0074 (grep: zero matches), its `related` names the superseded 0004 instead, and the README's non-supersession list (0023/0020, 0028/0029/0022, 0089/0067) does not carry the pair.

rows.title: Harness port shape unrealisable: sync blocking dispatch, a cancel handle no caller can hold, no channel for the dispatch record

anchors.quote: `dispatch(ActivitySpec) -> Result<Typed, StepError>`; capability registry with dated probes; cost/usage; **`cancel(handle)`**
Any port whose operations can be long-running exposes a cancel path that takes a handle minted when the operation started, and the adapter implements it as a real kill
pub async fn run(&self, spec: &StepSpec) -> (StepRecord, Result<serde_json::Value, StepError>) {
THEN exactly one dispatch event is appended carrying every token counter the harness reports verbatim, `total_cost_usd`,
THEN no function, struct or trait in `rk-kernel`'s public or internal API carries a generic type parameter bound by a port trait

rows.statement: Tracing kernel -> Harness -> `claude -p` -> result through the text: `dispatch` is a sync call that blocks the calling thread until the child exits, yet `cancel(handle)` takes a handle 'minted when the operation started' that no caller can obtain before `dispatch` returns; nothing names who calls cancel (a Ctrl-C handler, a wall-clock watchdog, a second thread) or from which thread. `Result<Typed, StepError>` also has no channel for the usage/headroom/effective-config record AC-360 requires on every termination path, whereas the runner the adapter lifts returns `(StepRecord, Result<..>)`. `ActivitySpec`, `Typed` and the handle type are never given fields, and `Typed` cannot be a per-call generic on an object-safe trait (AC-480).
rows.why_before_step5: `rk-ports` (Step 7a) declares this trait and Step 7c's acceptance set carries AC-224/AC-225/AC-360; two engineers would write incompatible traits (start/wait vs blocking dispatch, record-in-Ok vs adapter-appends-to-EventStore). It does not touch Step 5's `rk-types` except for the `StepError`/`ActivitySpec` field sets.
rows.remediation: Before 7a, record (a successor to ADR-0076 or a new record, never an edit): the trait as `dispatch(&ActivitySpec, &mut dyn EventStore) -> DispatchOutcome { record: DispatchRecord, result: Result<Typed, StepError> }` (or a `start() -> Handle` / `wait(Handle)` pair); a `CancelToken` cloned from the adapter before the call, owned by the composition root's signal/Ctrl-C handler and by the per-activity timeout; `Typed` as an erased validated value (`serde_json::Value` plus schema id) that the kernel deserialises; and the field sets of `ActivitySpec` (from `StepSpec`) and the record (from `StepRecord`).
rows.truth_reason: [measured] design:266 sketches `dispatch(ActivitySpec) -> Result<Typed, StepError>` plus `cancel(handle)`; ADR-0076:54 has the handle 'minted when the operation started' while :52 has the sync method block on the adapter's runtime; Consequences say only 'Timeouts move into adapters'. No text names an external caller or a handle-return channel. The runner has only the timeout kill (runner.rs:356-359); `Cancelled` is `dead_code` (step.rs:190). AC-360's kernel test over the EventStore fake needs the usage record in the kernel; the Result has no slot. `ActivitySpec`/`Typed` have no field set.
rows.material_reason: NEW: known-issues rows on cancel are the Windows handle leak (ARCH-10.4-030, ARCH-10.5-031, ARCH-10.x-T-021) and the sync-trait tension (ARCH-0.1-018); none records the dispatch/cancel/record shape gap. P1 stands: RUNBOOK 7a (line 1875) declares the trait and 7c's acceptance set carries AC-224/225/360; the shape as written cannot be implemented without a decision the corpus has not made. Not P0 — Step 5 is untouched beyond `StepError`/`ActivitySpec` fields.

rows.title: 'Process-group kill' has no Windows meaning; lifted runner uses taskkill /T; AC-225's exit-143 never holds on the build platform

anchors.quote: THEN the whole process group is killed and no descendant of the dispatch survives the call.
- **Instrument:** descendant PID count in the dispatch's process group (on Windows, its job object), sampled after cancel.
/// `taskkill /T /F`.
let _ = child.kill().await;
WHEN the child exits 143 with no result message
//! #24). Windows has no SIGTERM; `taskkill` without `/F` posts WM_CLOSE and
unsafe_code = "deny"

rows.statement: AC-224, ADR-0076 and §3.8.2 specify cancellation as a POSIX 'process-group kill'; SM-068 alone says 'on Windows, its job object'; the code §9.1 says 'survives unchanged inside rk-adapter-claude' does neither — on Windows it runs `taskkill /PID <pid> /T /F` (a parent-tree walk that needs the parent alive and misses re-parented grandchildren, i.e. the F22 survivor shape) and elsewhere `child.kill()`, which the file's own comment says reaches only the direct child. AC-225's GIVEN/WHEN ('exits 143') is SIGTERM semantics; measured here, a `taskkill /T /F` victim exits 1 [measured, this audit, Windows 11], so the classifier cannot use the exit code and must key on 'cancel was issued'. A Job Object with KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE needs FFI under a workspace-wide `unsafe_code = "deny"`.
rows.why_before_step5: Does not block Step 5. Blocks 7c: AC-224/AC-225 are in its acceptance set and the integration test 'asserts no live PID in the group' is unwritable until the containment primitive per OS is chosen.
rows.remediation: Record per-OS containment before 7c: Windows = Job Object created before spawn with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE (child assigned before it can fork; handle held by the adapter so parent death reaps the tree), POSIX = `CommandExt::process_group(0)` plus `killpg`; rewrite AC-225 as 'terminated by the adapter's own cancel' with the classifier keyed on the cancel token, not the exit code; enumerate the group via the job/pgid in the AC-224 test; grant the one commented `unsafe` override (or a safe wrapper crate) in `rk-adapter-claude`'s manifest per ADR-0083.
rows.truth_reason: Core holds: AC-224:2892, ADR-0076:54, design:393 say 'process group'; runner.rs:469-481 uses `taskkill /T /F` then `child.kill()`; taskkill victim exit re-measured = 1 on Windows 11 [measured]. But 'SM-068 alone says job object' is false: AC-278 verified-by (:3097) and the note at :3537 ('On Windows ... job-object containment is the reliable mechanism; if the implementation uses process groups the test may pass while a detached child survives') already record it. ADR-0083:68 pre-answers the unsafe point. AC-225's negative test already implies keying on our-own-cancel.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed (ARCH-10.4-030 / ADR-0076-FORB-78 cover the handle leak and the 'explicit kill' rule, not the per-OS primitive for AC-224). Priority down to P2: the job-object choice is already recorded at acceptance-criteria.md:3537 for the same F22 shape, ADR-0083:68 already licenses the unsafe override, and AC-225's negative test already forces cancel-token keying — 7c's author is fenced. What remains is record correctness (AC-224/ADR-0076 wording, AC-225's WHEN, §9.1 'survives unchanged').
rows.corrected_statement: AC-224, ADR-0076 §Decision and design §3.8.2 specify the adapter's cancel as a POSIX 'process-group kill'; the corpus knows Windows needs a Job Object (SM-068:528; AC-278 verified-by :3097; AC §note :3537) but says so only for AC-278/SM-068, never for AC-224, and the runner §9.1 says 'survives unchanged' in `rk-adapter-claude` does neither (runner.rs:470-481: `taskkill /PID /T /F` + `child.kill()`). AC-225's GIVEN/WHEN ('exits 143') is SIGTERM semantics that never obtains on Windows (taskkill /F victims exit 1 [measured]); the AC's negative test already implies keying on the adapter's own cancel, so the WHEN clause should be rewritten to match.

| A committed step is not re-dispatched — its memo key resolves — and the next action equals, under the canonical serialiser, the action an uninterrupted control run took at the same point | **AC-187**

| **Tier 1 — decision-bearing** | stage transitions, gate opened/answered, verdicts, slice seals | **git first**: trailers on a checkpoint commit, or an **empty commit** carrying the trailer when no checkpoint is due

rows.statement: A memo entry that stops a committed step from re-dispatching is decision-bearing by the design's own tier test ('if the database were deleted, would `redkiln run` take a different next action?'). The Step-5.3 hook is wrong: AC-160 is in Step 6's acceptance set (RUNBOOK.md:1863 'AC-160–AC-199'), not 5.3's (RUNBOOK.md:1771-1775, AC-120–AC-159). rows.title: Git is not a port and has no fake, yet replay binds every port to a fake — reconcile() and trailer writes under replay unspecified

anchors.quote: `cargo tree -i` assertion that returns empty. The workflow reaches the world only through `rk-ports` traits, so a
The port inventory lint carries a denylist over the git surface, and a declared `trait GitPort` is a compile-fail fixture (AC-483). `rk-kernel` depends on `rk-git` as a concrete crate.
WHEN the workflow is replayed against that log with every port bound to its fake
*Verified by:* `disallowed_methods`/`disallowed_types` over `rk-kernel::workflow` (`std::fs`, `std::process`,
kernel, through `rk-git`; the write path shells out to `git interpret-trailers --in-place` / `git commit --trailer`

rows.statement: The kernel writes tier-1 state (trailers, empty commits, worktrees) and reads decision state (reconcile()) through `rk-git`, a concrete crate that spawns `git` and calls gix. AC-005 says the workflow reaches the world only through `rk-ports` traits; AC-006/AC-008 replay by binding every port to its fake and serving N results from the journal. Git has no port, no fake and no journalled-result rule, so a replay either performs real git I/O (and real writes) or the git layer must be recorded/replayed by a mechanism nothing specifies. The clippy ban on `std::process` in the workflow module does not fire on a call into `rk-git`.
rows.why_before_step5: Not Step 5. Blocks 7b's replay suite (Phase-1 exit criterion 2) and shapes Step 6: whether `rk-git` needs a record/replay seam or git calls become journalled activities decides `rk-git`'s public API.
rows.remediation: Record before Step 6: git operations are activities on the activity side of the split — each `reconcile()` result and each write's outcome (sha, tree) is journalled and served from the journal under replay; `rk-git` exposes a `GitOps` seam (a struct, not a trait named as a port, so AC-483 stands) with a replaying implementation; AC-006/AC-008 gain the clause 'and zero `rk-git` writes'. Extend the AC-003 lint to a `cargo-deny`/module-boundary rule that only the activity module names `rk_git`.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] design:293 'rk-kernel depends on rk-git as a concrete crate'; AC-005:247; AC-006:254; AC-003:230 bans std::process only in `rk-kernel::workflow`. Nothing specifies git under replay. However AC-006's verified-by names 'the pinned corpus repo (ADR-0013)' as the replay substrate, so real git reads under replay are by design, and AC-172 (design:706, planner accepts only `Reconciled<State>`) already makes reconcile() a value input. The genuine gap narrows to the write side (trailers, empty commits, worktrees, merge) under replay and whether reconcile() results are journalled.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed (known-issues rk-git rows are all gix/common-dir: ARCH-1.3-004, ARCH-3.10-002, ARCH-5.11-002, ADR-0077-FORB-101). Priority down to P2: reads are already fenced (pinned corpus), reconcile() is already a value, and a replay can run writes in a disposable clone without any API change — a decision is owed but no Phase-1 crate is blocked on it.
rows.corrected_statement: Git is not a port and has no fake. AC-006/AC-008 replay 'with every port bound to its fake' over the pinned corpus repo, so git reads are real by design and reconcile() enters as a `Reconciled<State>` value (AC-172); but no document says whether tier-1 git writes (trailers, empty commits, worktree add/remove, merge landing) execute, are suppressed, or are journalled and served under replay, nor whether `rk-git` calls sit on the activity side of the split so that AC-003/AC-005 hold.

rows.title: gix/shell-out boundary imprecise: common-dir resolution, review-clone checkout, merge landing, checkpoint commits unassigned

anchors.quote: - `rev-parse`, including resolving the repository common dir that 0018 requires at startup;
| **S-GIX/a** | Against the pinned gix, can a store rooted at the git common dir be opened and written correctly from a linked worktree
taken by the facet-provenance amendment on 2026-09-09 and `0090` by Step 4.4. A **no-go** costs nothing, because
Restricting gix to reads also moves it away from `gix-worktree-state` checkout permissions, `gix-worktree` path traversal and Windows reserved-device-name handling

| **Read** | `gix`, at the exact pin `=0.87.1` | `rev-parse` (including resolving the common dir AC-178 requires at startup), repository and worktree status, **shallow clone by SHA** for review checkouts, **trailer parsing**
THEN they merge strictly one at a time
gix has named gaps in push maturity, full merge workflows, hooks and the common-dir interplay

rows.statement: Three imprecisions. (a) Resolving the common dir from a linked worktree is on gix's read side, but that resolution is the very `GIT_COMMON_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` interplay S-GIX/a tests, so a no-go on /a moves a read operation to the shell-out — the runbook's 'a no-go costs nothing' is wrong for arm /a. (b) 'Shallow clone by SHA for review checkouts' is listed as a read, but a reviewer needs files on disk, and a gix clone-with-checkout is a `gix-worktree-state` checkout — the surface the same paragraph says the read restriction moves gix away from. (c) The merge-queue landing (AC-196: 'they merge ... produced a commit and its trailer') and the checkpoint commit itself (`git add`/`git commit`) are writes absent from ADR-0077's write list, while ADR-0077 records gix 'gaps in full merge workflows'.
rows.why_before_step5: Not Step 5. Step 6 builds `rk-git` to the hybrid 'whatever S-GIX says' and Checkpoint 6 grep-asserts one shell-out file; without (a)-(c) settled, the single wrapper's operation list — and whether the review clone is bare — is guesswork.
rows.remediation: In the S-GIX successor record (RUNBOOK 6.1's next ADR): enumerate the wrapper's full write set — worktree add/remove, `git add`/`commit --trailer`, empty commits, `interpret-trailers`, merge/fast-forward on the integration ref, clone removal; state whether the review clone is created bare or checked out and by which implementation; and make S-GIX/a's no-go consequence explicit: common-dir resolution falls back to `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` through the wrapper.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] (a) ADR-0077:60 puts common-dir rev-parse on gix's read side; S-GIX/a (:78) tests that interplay and says 'the shell-out fallback is decided' though no shell-out rev-parse is in the Decision; AC-178:2403 and design:419 make `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` the oracle; RUNBOOK:1813 'A no-go costs nothing'; (b) design:743 lists shallow clone for review checkouts as a read while :746 moves gix away from `gix-worktree-state` checkout. (c) ADR-0077:64-66 lists only worktree add/remove and trailer writes; AC-196:2600-2604 has the queue 'produce a commit'; ADR-0077:25 notes merge gaps
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed (ARCH-5.11-002, ARCH-3.10-006, ARCH-10.5-006 record S-GIX and the hybrid, not (a)-(c)). Priority down to P2: ADR-0077's single-wrapper rule ('All shelling out goes through one wrapper type') is not an exhaustive operation list, so merge/checkpoint commits can be added without contradicting it; the hybrid ships on either S-GIX answer; Checkpoint 6's one-shell-out-file grep is satisfied regardless. RUNBOOK 6.1 already plans the successor record where (a)-(c) belong. Record correctness, not a blocked crate.

rows.title: Memo key under-specified: no hash framing, canonicalisation, 'toolchain version' meaning or schema version; two component lists

anchors.quote: | **Memo** | `hash(activity id, resolved inputs, card digest, **resolved** injected KB atoms, toolchain version)`
| | never silent | A memo hit appends a `memo_hit` event carrying the key and its five components; a skip is never invisible | AC-019; ADR-0036 |
unless the memo key (inputs, card digest, toolchain version, suite sha) is identical; a reuse is recorded as a memo hit with its key, never as a fresh run | AC-336 |
| `sha2` | 0.11.0 | caret | digests, memo keys, provenance | **proven** | `fingerprint::sha256_hex` [measured] |
| A `schema_version` per type; a schema change is a **migration** | design rule | schema-snapshot diff that fails an unversioned change

rows.statement: Two engineers computing `hash(...)` would disagree on: the serialisation of `resolved inputs` (the store's canonical serialiser is never named as the memo canonicaliser); component framing (length-prefixed vs concatenated); whether 'toolchain version' is the Toolchain port's `detect()` output, the pinned harness CLI version (AC-226) or the redkiln binary; and the loop counter — AC-017 puts it in the step key while AC-019 records 'five components'. §6.5's AC-336 states a different four-component key with `suite sha`. The output schema version is in no list, so a schema migration (AC-135) hits the memo and then fails AC-136's read instead of missing.
rows.why_before_step5: Not Step 5 (kernel, 7b), but the key is what AC-013/AC-187 resume and every memo test hinge on; an unpinned key silently changes hit rates between builds, which SM-001 would misread.
rows.remediation: Specify in the kernel area (an amendment record to ADR-0021, not an edit): SHA-256 over a length-prefixed, ordered tuple; `resolved inputs` canonicalised by `rk-store`'s canonical serialiser (sorted keys, fixed float format); `toolchain version` = the Toolchain adapter's detected version string plus `TESTED_CLI_VERSION`; add `output schema_version` and, for loop steps, the iteration tuple as named components; reconcile AC-019's 'five' and AC-336's four-tuple to the one list.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] design:322 and AC-014:330 give five components; AC-017:354-358 puts the loop counter in the step key; AC-019:373 records 'the key and its five components'; design:1014 gives AC-336 a four-tuple and AC-336:4166 itself a three-tuple (inputs, toolchain version, suite sha) — even that pair disagrees. No text names the hash framing, the canonicalisation of `resolved inputs`, or what 'toolchain version' denotes (grep over design/ADR-0021/ADR-0073: none). Minor overreach: AC-336 is the verify-area evidence key, arguably a different key sharing the name.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed: known-issues memo rows (ADR-0021-FORB-44/45, ADR-0028-NEG-50, SM-5.1-001/009/047, AC-15.3-013) cover loop-awareness, subgraph hashing and unmeasured hit rates, not key framing or the five-vs-six component count. P2 is right — record correctness with a later-build consequence (AC-013/AC-187 tests, SM-001 comparability), no Phase-1 crate blocked.

rows.title: 'One SQLite writer' is per connection not per store: no busy_timeout value, no transaction bound, queue conflicts with AC-360

anchors.quote: sets `journal_mode = WAL` and a `busy_timeout`, and uses **a single writer connection or a queued write path** — never a connection pool expecting parallel writes.
- The store lives at `<git-common-dir>/redkiln/` and is shared across worktrees (0003, 0018), so multi-process access is the normal case, not an edge case.
| Two processes in two worktrees both land their writes, with no lock error and one store file | **AC-181**
AND no dispatch path exists that can terminate without appending that event.
Concurrency across ports is the composition root's job — expressed as threads or an adapter-internal concurrent call

rows.statement: The writer rule constrains connections inside one process; the multi-process case ADR-0084 calls 'the normal case' is serialised only by SQLite's file lock and `busy_timeout`, whose value appears nowhere, and no bound is placed on the longest write transaction (`doctor --rebuild`, a migration) that another process must wait out to satisfy AC-181's 'no lock error'. The permitted 'queued write path' makes append asynchronous relative to dispatch termination, so an F22-class kill can drop a queued event — violating AC-360's 'no dispatch path can terminate without appending'. Since a rusqlite `Connection` is not `Sync`, the composition-root threads of §3.8.1 force a choice between mutex and queue that is left open.
rows.why_before_step5: Not Step 5. Bounds `rk-adapter-sqlite` (7c) and the AC-181/AC-360 tests; R-SQLITE's contention test cannot be written without the timeout and transaction-length numbers.
rows.remediation: With R-SQLITE, record: the `busy_timeout` value and the rule that every write transaction is shorter than it (rebuild runs in a separate database file then renames); one writer connection per process behind a mutex, no queue, so append is synchronous with the dispatch path; add to AC-181 a long-transaction fixture; state that concurrent items are separate processes rather than threads of one writer.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] ADR-0084:71 permits 'a single writer connection or a queued write path'; ADR-0084:34 calls multi-process access the normal case; grep over references/ and RUNBOOK finds `busy_timeout` 14 times with no numeric value and no transaction-length bound; AC-360:4469 'no dispatch path exists that can terminate without appending'; AC-181 (design:721) requires 'no lock error' across two processes. The queue-vs-AC-360 tension under an F22-class kill is a fair inference; the rusqlite `Connection: !Sync` point is standard and forces the mutex-vs-queue choice the ADR leaves open.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed: ARCH-9.4-002 / ARCH-10.4-015 / ADR-0084-NEG-90 / ADR-0084-FORB-99 record the single-writer rule as UNVERIFIED with R-SQLITE owed, but none records the missing timeout value, transaction bound, or the queue-vs-AC-360 conflict. P2 sound — bounds 7c's `rk-adapter-sqlite` and the AC-181/AC-360 tests, nothing blocked; R-SQLITE is the natural home for the numbers.

`std::env::set_var` is not called anywhere in the workspace, in tests included; a test that needs different configuration constructs a different `Config`.

*Verified by:* unit test that spawns with a key set in the parent and asserts refusal; an assertion on the constructed

rows.statement: §9.6 lands `hygiene.rs` in `rk-adapter-claude`; that file reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the process environment, and §9.1/AC-488 say the adapter 'refuses construction when ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is present' — a second environment read outside the composition root. rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN, not NEW: design:1661 and RUNBOOK:1702-1705 record the uninstrumented convention (the census did not row it, but the corpus does). Priority down to P3: convention/hygiene with a one-line remediation ('adapters take an `Environment` value'), no test that cannot compile, no crate blocked.

rows.title: Card body, JSON schema and agent card ride on argv under the ~32 KB cap the design cites; nothing bounds the command line

anchors.quote: | **Prompt on stdin, never argv** | A Windows command line caps near 32 KB; the `redkiln-review` card alone is 6.6 KB and the fix-lane prompt bodies are larger. Argv works in testing and fails on a real review | `rk-adapter-claude`

The Harness adapter's Phase-1 default is the static `--system-prompt` carrying the card body, with `--append-system-prompt` / `--exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections` absent from argv (AC-211, PROVISIONAL
args.push("--json-schema".into());
args.push(card.to_agents_json());
"ignored when `--system-prompt` or `--system-prompt-file` is set."

rows.statement: The design's Phase-1 card delivery is `--system-prompt <card body>` on argv; the lifted runner also passes the whole agent card as `--agents <json>` and the output schema as `--json-schema <json>` on argv. All of these share the command-line cap that §9.6 gives as the reason the prompt goes on stdin (the review card alone is 6.6 KB; skills compiled into the card prefix and the `Findings` schema grow it further). No criterion, lint or builder assertion bounds the assembled argv, and the `--system-prompt-file` route the grounding pass recorded is never considered.

anchors.quote: | `rk-cli` | `clap` router; one idempotent `run` entry; `answer`, `status`, `doctor`. **The composition root** | new | Yes (it constructs adapters)
| `tokio` | 1.53.1 | caret | **adapter crates only** | **proven** | ADR-0076 forbids it in `rk-kernel`/`rk-ports`/`rk-types` |
the async runtime exists in exactly the crates that spawn processes or open sockets. Each is a manifest-level fact a reviewer can check by reading `Cargo.toml`.
| `rk-git` | trailers, `reconcile()`, worktrees, disposable clones, merge queue | `reconcile.rs` rewritten in the spike + new | No |

[workspace.lints.clippy]

rows.statement: `disallowed_methods`/`disallowed_types` are configured in `clippy.toml`, which applies to a whole crate (or workspace), not to a module; the `[workspace.lints]` table RUNBOOK 5.1 writes cannot carry them, and neither ADR-0083's Decision nor any runbook step creates a `clippy.toml`. rows.title: Parallel antichains: threads or processes unstated; collides differently with the single writer and F22; sets port Send/Sync

anchors.quote: | **Parallel across project-DAG antichains** | One worktree per concurrent story — **required, not an optimisation**

Concurrency across ports is the composition root's job — expressed as threads or an adapter-internal concurrent call, with results entering the kernel as values in a defined order, so the kernel never observes interleaving.

- A single writer connection is a throughput ceiling. Under the "one machine per repo" operating assumption (0003) that ceiling is far away, but it is a real one and it will be reached first by a fan-out that ignores 0076's rule about where concurrency lives.

rows.statement: `redkiln run <item>` is item-scoped and exits at gates; §7.7 requires concurrent stories in separate worktrees; ADR-0076 says fan-out is 'threads' at the composition root. Nothing says whether N concurrent stories are N kernels on N threads sharing one process's single writer connection (needing the queued write path finding 08 shows is unsafe under a kill) or N processes (each a background job of the shape F22 measured dying). Phase 1 ships single-lane runs, so this is not a Phase-1 blocker, but the thread model it implies leaks into the port trait (`Send`/`Sync` bounds on `dyn Harness`, `dyn EventStore`).
rows.why_before_step5: Not Step 5; noted because 7a must choose `Send`/`Sync` bounds on the port trait objects, and the wrong choice is a breaking change later.
rows.remediation: Record the Phase-2 shape now as a one-line consequence in a new record: one process per concurrent story, launched and reaped by a foreground supervisor (never `Start-Process`), each with its own writer connection; port trait objects declared `Send` but not required `Sync`.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] design:1167, design:383 / ADR-0076:56 and ADR-0084:91 read as quoted. But the finding conflates two levels: ADR-0076's fan-out is across ports within one kernel operation, while §7.7's antichain parallelism is across items, and the corpus already models the latter as separate processes — `redkiln run <item>` is item-scoped and exits at gates, 'nothing waits' (design:1160), and AC-181 (design:721) is written for 'two processes in two worktrees'. What survives is that port trait objects' `Send`/`Sync` bounds are unstated anywhere [grep].
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed (ARCH-10.4-018 covers fan-out timing only). P3 stands; Phase 2 concern by the finder's own admission, and the surviving remediation is one sentence on trait-object bounds at 7a. Borderline immaterial; retained only for that sentence.
rows.corrected_statement: Concurrent stories are implicitly separate `redkiln run` processes (item-scoped run, AC-181's two-process fixture, one worktree per story), not threads of one kernel; the corpus never says so in one place, and never states the `Send`/`Sync` bounds on the `dyn` port objects that 7a must fix.

rows.statement: [documented] ADR-0007 records that no criterion defines an S-CODEX pass. rows.title: 'Roughly 60 positives are needed for a lower bound above 0.95' — the exact minimum at k=n is 73; at n=60 the bound is 0.940

rows.statement: Solving Wilson(k=n) lower > 0.95 at z=1.96 gives n=73 as the first n that clears it (n=60: 0.9398, n=70: 0.9480, n=72: 0.9493, n=73: 0.9500) [measured]. rows.title: F37 §2 overlap arithmetic wrong: 3/3 [0.44,1.00] and 0/3 [0.00,0.56] overlap, so §4.4(1) is strictly unfalsifiable at n=3
rows.known_issue_match: F37-LIM-001 / F37-LIMP-001 (spikes/F37-DRAFT.md:131 'close to unfalsifiable'); ARCH-1.2-011 and ARCH-0.1-006 ('overlaps by construction')

anchors.quote: With n=3, a 3/3 cell has a Wilson interval of [0.44, 1.00] and a 0/3 cell has [0.00, 0.56]; the only way two such cells fail to overlap is a 3/3 against a 0/3, which is the maximum possible separation.
1. **n=3 per cell.** Every Wilson interval is wide enough that §4.4's first criterion is close to unfalsifiable (§2). This is the dominant limit.

rows.statement: The two intervals F37 itself quotes share [0.44, 0.56]; 3/3 = (0.4385, 1.0) and 0/3 = (0, 0.5615) [measured]. Since that is the maximum possible separation at n=3, no outcome of the P7 run could have made §4.4's first criterion not fire — it is unfalsifiable, not 'nearly unearnable' or 'close to unfalsifiable'. F37's own headline (line 1) and the design/RUNBOOK ('overlaps by construction') say the stronger, correct thing; §2 and Limits 1 contradict it with a false arithmetic claim.
rows.why_before_step5: Strengthens, not weakens, the corpus's conclusion that P7 §4.4(1) carries no verdict; the quality-shorthand default stays BLOCKED either way. Record correctness inside the spike that the ADR-0080 block decision cites.
rows.remediation: Amend F37 §2 and Limits 1 (do not edit the METHOD): 'at n=3 no two Wilson intervals can be disjoint; the criterion cannot fail to fire at this n.' Keep the headline as is.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. METHOD-P.md:17 fixes Wilson 95%; at 95% 3/3=[0.4385,1.0] and 0/3=[0,0.5615] share [0.44,0.56] [measured], so F37 section 2's 'only way two such cells fail to overlap is 3/3 against 0/3' is false on its own numbers, and 'can only detect an effect that is total' is also false (it detects nothing). rows.title: F19 3.6x: ratio correct (3.61) but 'overlapping intervals, not separated' is the CI-overlap fallacy; direct test p=0.04
rows.known_issue_match: none (RB-GC-010 and SM §0 rule 3 cite the overlap as a recorded failure mode; no row questions the inference)

anchors.quote: **The 3.6× ratio is a point estimate and those two intervals overlap — the ratio is not separated at this n.**
**the two conditional intervals overlap**, so 3.6× is a point estimate on one operator's single repository, not a separated effect [measured, F19; intervals recomputed in the AC pass]
F19's 3.6× duration effect on drift has overlapping conditional intervals (1.1–8.9% vs 6.1–20.3%) and is directional only

rows.statement: 9/79 vs 3/95: RR = 3.61 [measured]; no interval on the ratio is given anywhere. Log-RR 95% CI is [1.01, 12.9]; Fisher exact two-sided p = 0.039; two-proportion z p = 0.033; Newcombe difference CI [0.4%, 17.3%] — all exclude the null at 95%, narrowly. Overlap of two separate 95% intervals does not imply non-separation (the joint test is less conservative), so 'not separated at this n' is a mis-inference, in the conservative direction. Minor: SM :923 and :1182 print the >1 h upper bound as 20.2% while 9/79 gives 0.20255 → 20.3% (design :712/:866 have 20.3%).
rows.why_before_step5: No build impact: eager reconcile() is justified by the 7% overall rate regardless. It matters only because the register's doctrine §0 rule 3 uses this inference as its paradigm example of small-n discipline, and the paradigm is a known fallacy; the honest wording is 'separated only marginally (p≈0.04) on one operator's repository'.
rows.remediation: Reword SM :18, :923 and design :712 to report the ratio with its CI [1.0, 12.9] and 'marginal at n=174, one operator', instead of inferring non-separation from overlap; fix 20.2% → 20.3%.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. RR=3.608, log-RR 95% CI [1.01, 12.87]; Fisher two-sided p=0.039; two-proportion z p=0.033 [measured]. The corpus asserts 'not separated at this n' from interval overlap; overlap of two separate 95% intervals does not establish non-separation, and direct tests separate at 0.05, marginally. 'Directional only, one operator' is a defensible summary; the stated reason is a fallacy. Also: 9/79 upper = 0.20255 -> 20.3%; SM :18 and :399 print 20.3% (:399 'confirmed exact') while SM :923, :925, :1182 print 20.2% [measured].
rows.material_reason: known-issues rows ARCH-0.1-021 (design :39) and RB-GC-010 quote the 3.6x/overlap statement as fact; SM-3.4-008 records a different overlap case (SM-021). No row questions the inference; the anomaly_pool '3.6' hit is the unrelated 3.66x/4.4x P7 cost dispute. NEW confirmed. P3 is right: the error is in the conservative direction and eager reconcile() rests on the 7% overall rate; remediation value is real but small (reword SM :18/:923 and design :712; fix the 20.2/20.3 inconsistency at SM :923/:925/:1182).

arrives on `rate_limit_event`, **not** on a failure result — the adapter must derive `RateLimited { resets_at }` from
THEN the dispatch resolves to `StepError::Platform { status, retry_after }` — the exit code is not consulted to overturn it.

`Transport` / `Platform` 5xx / `Timeout`: exponential backoff with full jitter, base 2 s, cap 5 min, ≤ the pack's `N`. `RateLimited { resets_at }`: **no sleep** — write a `retry_at(resets_at)` mark and exit 0.

rows.statement: The design handles headroom before spawn (AC-220 margin refusal) and `RateLimited { resets_at }` derived from `rate_limit_event` (AC-030/AC-222), but a window that runs out while an 18-minute review is in flight surfaces as a `result` carrying `is_error`/text, which AC-218 classifies as `Platform` and §3.6 retries with 2 s-to-5 min backoff up to N — against a reset hours away. The spike runner's `StepError::UsageLimit` and its `detect_usage_limit` substring match ("usage limit reached", "you've hit your", ...) exist precisely because the charter records no structured subtype, yet no design `StepError` variant, AC or S-RETRY arm names the exhaustion-on-result surface [measured: 0 hits for usage limit/plan limit/UsageLimit in the design, AC and ADR sets], and ADR-0010's Negative consequences list only the CI gap.
rows.why_before_step5: Subscription-only (ADR-0010) makes window exhaustion the primary operational failure of every run; Step 7c lifts runner.rs 'unchanged' with a text detector the design's own no-prose-parsing principles do not licence, and the kernel's closed `StepError` (AC-229) has no arm for it. Either the variant is decided before the adapter is built or the attempts budget is silently spent on immediate re-failures.
rows.remediation: Add an AC in the harness area (AC-200..239 has ids free) that a child terminating with a usage-limit result resolves to `RateLimited { resets_at }` (with `resets_at` from the last `rate_limit_event` in the same stream, else the pack delay), name the detection surface explicitly (structured `subtype` first, text markers as a disclosed fallback recorded on the event), and extend S-RETRY's registered question to cover exhaustion-on-result, not only the throttle margin.

Nuance: whether exhaustion sets is_error is undocumented (charter:96); the defect stands on either surface.

rows.title: AC-068's unblocking precondition exits 0 only where METHOD-P §2.4 prescribes no stale_policy, and reads a record nothing writes

anchors.quote: #   AND rec.recall/rec.precision clear P2's PRE-REGISTERED lines.
redkiln lint --stale-policy .redkiln/packs --p2-record spikes/results/p2/shortcircuit.json

- Coarse `derived_from`: **recall < 0.9** or **precision < 0.7** → fine scope becomes mandatory for `L`-class activities and `stale_policy = gate` is the default for them.

rows.statement: AC-068 tests the `stale_policy = gate` branch and is PROVISIONAL until its lint exits 0, which requires recall/precision to 'clear' (§1.2: 'clear or fail') §2.4's lines. But §2.4 prescribes `stale_policy = gate` only when those lines are NOT cleared (criterion 1 fires); when they are cleared it prescribes nothing. So after P2-B the precondition unblocks the gate criterion exactly when the pre-registration gives no warrant for gating, and can never exit 0 in the outcome the criterion exists for. Separately, the record it reads (`spikes/results/p2/shortcircuit.json` with `labels_timestamped`, `n_items`, `recall`) is written by nothing: score-p2.py prints only, and the engine writes p2-engine.jsonl [measured].
rows.why_before_step5: No Step-5 impact (the setting is blocked and the lint is Phase-1 tooling), but whoever writes `redkiln lint --stale-policy` from this text will build a check whose pass condition is the negation of the decision rule it is meant to enforce.
rows.remediation: Amend AC-068's precondition to: exit 0 only when rec.labels_timestamped, rec.n_cases >= 20 with a positive class present (recall has a denominator), AND every pack's declared `stale_policy` per class matches what §2.4's fired/unfired criteria prescribe. Name the record an instrument will write (extend score-p2.py with --out, or name p2-engine.jsonl) and mark it [WILL EXIST].
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. The inversion holds: AC:182 pairs 'clear or fail', so clear = pass; METHOD-P §2.4:149 prescribes stale_policy = gate only when criterion 1 fires (criterion 2's 'either' presupposes it failed), so a record clearing both lines prescribes no gate while one that fires them exits non-zero. The phantom record is real — score-p2.py has only --engine/--labels, no writer [measured] — but not P2-specific: AC-071 at AC:161 names spikes/results/p1/stability.json, equally unwritten. `--stale-policy` appears only at AC:939; no RUNBOOK step builds it.
rows.material_reason: NEW — no known-issues row mentions shortcircuit.json, --stale-policy, or the clear/fire inversion; AC-PROV-008 records line 1285's status change, not this. P2 stands as a record-correctness defect, but 'whoever writes redkiln lint --stale-policy ... will build a check whose pass condition is the negation' overstates: nothing in RUNBOOK builds that lint. Remediation should cover AC-068's and AC-071's phantom records together.
rows.corrected_statement: AC-068's executable precondition exits 0 only when recall/precision 'clear' METHOD-P §2.4's lines — the case in which §2.4 prescribes no stale_policy — and exits non-zero when the criteria fire and prescribe one; the pass condition is the negation of the decision rule. The record it reads (spikes/results/p2/shortcircuit.json) is written by no instrument, a convention it shares with AC-071's spikes/results/p1/stability.json (AC:161); neither is marked [WILL EXIST]. No RUNBOOK step schedules `redkiln lint --stale-policy`, so the inversion has no Phase-1 build consequence.

rows.title: AC-067's trigger 'an upstream artifact it would conceptually depend on' has no definition for a vouched root whose derived_from is empty

anchors.quote: WHEN an upstream artifact it would conceptually depend on changes
When an upstream artifact in the same stage subsequently changes, the *next* gate the item reaches carries an advisory note

The reconstruction — "which upstream file changed before this artifact was last written" (§2.2) — is picking the card up as a derivation edge because the card is rewritten so often that it is nearly always the most recent prior write.

rows.statement: A vouched root records `derived_from = []`, so the engine has no declared edge to test drift against. ADR-0025 bounds it to 'an upstream artifact in the same stage'; AC-067 drops 'same stage' and says 'would conceptually depend on'. Three buildable readings: (a) any same-stage artifact written after the root; (b) the `requires` of the kind's registered producer, which a `source = "human"` kind need not have (ADR-0057); (c) a most-recent-prior-write reconstruction, which F40 measured as the noisier scope. AC-067's Verified-by (a unit test on 'the vouched-root path') cannot discriminate among them.
rows.why_before_step5: The advisory path is the half of step 3 that ships unit-tested in Phase 1; which reading is built decides SM-022's event volume and whether the advisory becomes the 'noise' ADR-0025 records as unmeasured.
rows.remediation: Amend AC-067's WHEN to name the edge set — 'an artifact of a kind listed in the registered producer's `requires` for the root's kind, in the same stage (ADR-0025), changes digest' — and add a fixture where a same-stage artifact outside that set changes and no advisory is emitted.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. AC-067's WHEN (AC:916) says 'an upstream artifact it would conceptually depend on'; ADR-0025:39 bounds it to 'an upstream artifact in the same stage' and its Consequences (line 45) say the human 'is not asked to pre-declare its dependencies', so no declared edge set exists for a `derived_from = []` root; AC-053 (AC:763) says human-supplied kinds are 'source nodes with no producer', so a producer's `requires` need not exist. All three readings fit the text, and AC-067's Verified-by (AC:920) is a negative co-occurrence assertion that cannot discriminate among them.
rows.material_reason: known-issues carries ADR-0025's NEG/FORB rows and its [unmeasured] noise-rate line (ADR-0025:62) and SM-5.1-010 (SM-022 needs 50 advisories); none records that the trigger edge set is undefined. *Verified by:* unit test on the vouched-root path; an event-log assertion that `drift_advisory` never co-occurs with a
THEN it stays `Present`, its producer is not dispatched, and any drift signal is written as an **advisory** that does not

rows.title: ADR-0087 'costs less than a stage gate' divides P8 output tokens by F28 cache-creation tokens; SM-073 baseline is not its instrument

- Forbids avoiding a mid-graph gate on the stated grounds that it costs more than a stage gate — measured, it costs less.

rows.statement: F28's ~18,603 is `cache_creation_input_tokens` on a post-TTL re-read of a warmed prefix (creation was 0 at 0.9 min). F38's 8,408 / 10,314 / 14,579 are summed `output_tokens` of the resumed `attempt` dispatch: the driver sums `u.output_tokens` and divides by a hard-coded 18600. The 0.45x/0.55x/0.78x ratio therefore compares unlike quantities, with all three draws inside the TTL where the like-for-like F28 figure would be ~0. ADR-0087 decision clause 3 and its forbids line, SM-073's baseline (instrument = cache_creation_input_tokens, baseline = output tokens) and AC-266's provisional note all restate the ratio as a measured cost comparison. METHOD-P §5.4 pre-registered 'resume cost in tokens' without fixing the token type.
rows.why_before_step5: The build is unaffected (AC-266's test is apples-to-apples), but SM-073, one of the three discriminating human-gate measures, would compare its first production reading against a baseline of a different quantity; ADR-0087 forbids a design choice on a comparison that was never made; and P8-B, the registered unblock, inherits the same driver metric.
rows.remediation: Supersede ADR-0087 partially (never edit): withdraw clause 3's 'measured, it costs less' and the matching forbids line, restating the F38 cost result as 'output tokens of the resumed step, not comparable to F28's cache-creation figure; cost ordering UNMEASURED'. Amend METHOD-P §5.4 by dated note fixing the token type for P8-B (cache_creation_input_tokens and total_cost_usd, per SM-073). Re-baseline SM-073 as 'no baseline' and correct AC-266's provisional note.
rows.owner: Ryan Britton (ADR-0087 successor; METHOD-P amendment; SM-073)

FINDINGS:1714-1718 table header is 'cache creation on resume' and 18,603 is that column at 65.2 min; F38:33 header is 'resume output tokens'; main.rs:3288 sums u.output_tokens and :3349 divides by a hard-coded 18600.0. The ratio compares unlike quantities exactly as stated.

rows.statement: Two readings: (1) the adapter reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the process environment at construction and the unit test sets it with `std::env::set_var`, the AC's literal instrument, forbidden by ADR-0083 and `unsafe` in edition 2024; (2) the parent environment is captured once in `rk-cli`'s `Config` and the adapter asserts on a map it is handed, so the test constructs a `Config`, consistent with ADR-0083 and RUNBOOK 7d but not what either AC's 'Verified by' says. AC-217's 'siblings' of `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is also unenumerated, so two implementers would refuse on different variable sets.
rows.why_before_step5: Bites at Step 7c (adapters) and Step 5.2 CI (the set_var lint), not Step 5.1; left as written, the first test an implementer writes for AC-217 fails the workspace lint.
rows.remediation: Amend AC-217 and AC-488's 'Verified by' to 'a unit test constructing a `Config` whose captured environment carries the key, asserting the typed error and dispatch count 0'; add 'the adapter never reads the process environment; it receives the captured map as a value'; enumerate the sibling variable names.
rows.truth_reason: All five anchors verbatim [measured]. But the conflict holds only under reading (1): AC-217's 'spawns with a key set in the parent' and AC-488's 'a unit test with the variable set' do not mandate std::env::set_var — a test may spawn a helper via Command::env, or hand the adapter a Config whose captured map carries the key, both consistent with ADR-0083:76. An under-specified instrument, not a contradiction, and the bad reading is fenced by ADR-0083's lint. The 'siblings' point stands: no document enumerates them (grep of ADR-0010, design, ACs, RUNBOOK: only ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is named).

rows.title: S-GIX/a tests an operation the hybrid keeps on gix's READ path, so 'a no-go costs nothing' is false and no fallback is written
rows.known_issue_match: none (ARCH-10.4-012 / ARCH-1.3-004 record the gap; neither records that the gap sits on the gix read path)

anchors.quote: - `rev-parse`, including resolving the repository common dir that 0018 requires at startup;

does the `GIT_COMMON_DIR`/`GIT_WORK_TREE` interplay behave, or is `crate-status.md` still accurate? | `rk-git` worktree lifecycle | **No** — the shell-out fallback is decided. It gates only the *narrowing*. |
A **no-go** costs nothing, because
| **Read** | `gix`, exact pin `= "=0.87.1"` | `rev-parse` (including resolving the common dir AC-178 needs at startup)
GIVEN a linked worktree of a repository

rows.statement: S-GIX/a asks whether the common dir can be resolved and the store opened from a linked worktree — i.e. whether the GIT_COMMON_DIR/GIT_WORK_TREE interplay works in gix — yet ADR-0077 §Decision and RUNBOOK 6.2 assign exactly that operation (rev-parse incl. common-dir resolution at startup, AC-178) to gix's read path, which the hybrid does NOT fall back from. A no-go on S-GIX/a therefore leaves gix owning the operation the arm just falsified, while ADR-0077, §5.9 and RUNBOOK 6.1 all say the arm 'gates only the narrowing' and 'a no-go costs nothing'. Conversely the arm never exercises the ops it could narrow (gix worktree add/remove), so a go licenses nothing the forbids block names.
rows.why_before_step5: Step 6 runs S-GIX/a first and then builds rk-git 'to the hybrid, whatever S-GIX says'. On a no-go the implementer following the RUNBOOK would ship gix common-dir resolution from linked worktrees — the AC-178 startup path on which every worktree's store access depends — with the spike result in hand saying it does not work, and no written fallback to reach for.
rows.remediation: Successor record (ADR-0091, never an edit to 0077): restate S-GIX/a as a READ-path check whose no-go moves common-dir resolution (`git rev-parse --git-common-dir`) into the exec wrapper, and whose go confirms gix for that op; define separately what, if anything, would narrow 'no gix for worktree add/remove' (gix has no worktree-add API to test). Amend RUNBOOK 6.1/6.2 to replace 'a no-go costs nothing' with the two outcomes.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] All five anchors verbatim. ADR-0077:60 and RUNBOOK:1820 assign rev-parse incl. common-dir resolution to gix; ADR-0077:78 and design §5.9 (line 749) define S-GIX/a as opening a store at the common dir from a linked worktree, i.e. the same resolution; §5.9 Read row says 'Nothing contradicts the read-side bet' while its Write row cites the common-dir gap as basis. No fallback for common-dir resolution exists anywhere (forbids block, 6.2, AC-178). The 'decided fallback' rationale for 'Gates Phase 1? No' does not cover arm a.
