rows.title: The trailer write contract inherits ambient git config; S-GIX/b's byte-identity oracle and fixture set are unspecified

anchors.quote: - `git interpret-trailers --in-place` and/or `git commit --trailer` for every trailer write.
Two git implementations live in one process, and they can disagree — notably about config resolution and path handling on Windows.
does a five-line unit test round-trip a trailer **byte-identically** to `git interpret-trailers --in-place`? | `rk-git` trailer write path — **tier-1 state** |

rows.statement: Both named write commands honour the operator's and repository's `trailer.*` config (`trailer.ifexists`, `trailer.where`, `trailer.separators`, per-token variants) plus `commit.cleanup`, `core.commentChar` and `i18n.commitEncoding`; nothing in ADR-0077, §5.9, the ACs or RUNBOOK 6.2 says the wrapper pins these (`-c trailer.ifexists=add`, `-c trailer.separators=:`, `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL`/`GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM`). Two implementers: one inherits config (a repo with `trailer.ifexists=replace` silently collapses a second `Story:` trailer; a changed separator makes the trailer invisible to gix's fixed-`:` parser and to F12's 'column-anchored' reconcile), the other pins it. The S-GIX/b oracle is the same config-dependent command, and 'a five-line unit test' names no fixture (existing trailer block, no trailing newline, `---` divider, CRLF, duplicate token), so a 'go' from one default-config round-trip is weak evidence for tier-1 writes.
rows.why_before_step5: Not a Step-5 blocker; it becomes the wrapper's contract at Step 6, where the ADR itself calls a silently-wrong trailer write 'a state-corruption class, not a bug class'.
rows.remediation: In the S-GIX successor record or a new AC under §6.1: the git-exec wrapper runs every trailer write with trailer-affecting config pinned via `-c`, and S-GIX/b's oracle runs under the same pinned config over a named fixture matrix; add an AC asserting gix-parsed == git-written for each fixture.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] Anchors 68, 92 (ADR-0077) and RUNBOOK:1799 verbatim. grep of RUNBOOK, references/ and the spike planning docs for trailer.ifexists|trailer.where|trailer.separators|commit.cleanup|core.commentChar|i18n.commitEncoding returns hits only inside spikes/fixtures (old-redkiln command files), none in the design, ADR, AC register or RUNBOOK; the S-GIX/b oracle is the same config-honouring command and no fixture is named. The ambiguity is real and [inferred] as the finder tagged it.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed: ADR-0077-NEG-91 (ADR-0077:92) records gix-vs-git disagreement on config resolution; nothing records that the write command itself is config-dependent or that the spike oracle inherits the same config. P2 is right: no Step-5 impact, a contract clause for the Step 6 wrapper on tier-1 state.

rows.title: Repository hooks run on every exec-wrapper trailer commit; the corpus's 'no hooks' rule covers only redkiln-authored hooks

anchors.quote: THEN nothing has been written under the repository's `hooks/` directory
gix has named gaps in push maturity, full merge workflows, hooks and the common-dir interplay
AND if the git write fails the store contains no row for that transition.

rows.statement: Shelling out to `git commit --trailer` (unlike gix, which the ADR notes does not run hooks) executes the target repository's pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg and post-commit hooks (or `core.hooksPath`) on every tier-1 transition commit. The corpus rules only that redkiln writes no hooks (AC-182, AC-412). A commitlint/husky commit-msg hook rejecting a trailer-only message fails every transition (AC-162 then leaves no store row, so the item cannot advance); a prepare-commit-msg hook can rewrite the message and drop the trailer — the silent-wrong-write class the ADR names. Whether the wrapper passes `--no-verify` (which skips pre-commit and commit-msg but not prepare-commit-msg/post-commit) or overrides `core.hooksPath` is undecided.
rows.why_before_step5: No Step-5 impact; it is a missing clause in the Step 6 wrapper contract and a missing AC in §6.1, cheap to add now and expensive to discover on the first self-hosted repo with hooks.
rows.remediation: Add to the successor record and an AC: the wrapper runs trailer commits with `-c core.hooksPath=<empty dir>` (or documents `--no-verify` and the residual prepare-commit-msg exposure) and AC-162's fault-injection fixture includes a rejecting commit-msg hook and a message-rewriting prepare-commit-msg hook.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] Anchors AC:2440, ADR-0077:25, AC:2251 verbatim. Every 'hook' mention in the planning corpus (design:722/2046, AC:1744/2442, ADR-0018:34/57, evidence-augmentation) concerns redkiln writing no hooks or git-branchless #1334; none addresses repository-authored hooks firing on the exec wrapper's git commit --trailer. AC-182's verified-by ('identical output ... with it present') tacitly assumes hooks are inert. [inferred] --no-verify semantics and the prepare-commit-msg residue are standard git behaviour.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed: no known-issues row and no anomaly_pool entry mentions hook execution on shell-out commits. P2 is right: a missing clause in the Step 6 wrapper contract and a missing AC-162 fault-injection case; not a Step-5 or workstream blocker.

rows.title: ADR-0077's read/write split is an enumerated list, not a rule: patch-id, worktree prune, merge-queue merges and cat-file have no owner

anchors.quote: **gix owns the read path**, at the exact pin recorded in 0084:
GIVEN an orphaned anchor whose successor commit is identified by a recorded mechanism (patch-id equality, `ORIG_HEAD`,
*Verified by:* an integration test that `rm -rf`s a worktree and `git worktree prune`s, asserting zero new orphans and a
WHEN the merge produces a tree different from the tree the verdict was issued against

rows.statement: ADR-0077 assigns four read ops to gix and two write op families to the exec wrapper, and its forbids block only forbids gix for worktree add/remove and trailer writes. The ACs need more: AC-169's patch-id mechanism (git has `git patch-id`; gix has none), AC-190's `git worktree prune`, AC-292's `cat-file -e`, SM-054's `rev-list --count --all`, and the merge queue's merge/ref update (AC-196/197, Phase 2) — for which the ADR's own context says gix has 'named gaps in full merge workflows'. Two implementers reading 'gix owns the read path' diverge: one reimplements patch-id over gix diffs (divergence risk from git's algorithm), the other shells out reads through a wrapper the ADR describes as owning the write path; one merges via gix::merge (not forbidden), the other via `git merge`.
rows.why_before_step5: Reconcile (AC-167..170) is Step 6 code; the rule needs stating before it is built so the wrapper's scope is a principle ('git executes every mutation of .git and every op gix does not expose at the pin') rather than a list.
rows.remediation: Successor record: state the split as a rule with the four/two lists as examples, name patch-id and worktree prune as exec-wrapper ops, and record that merge-queue merges (Phase 2) go through the wrapper unless a later spike says otherwise.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] Anchors verbatim. But three of the five 'unowned' ops are test-harness or instrument invocations, not product operations: AC-190's `git worktree prune` and AC-292's `git cat-file -e` sit in *Verified by:* clauses (AC:2534, AC:3693); SM-054's `rev-list --count --all` is the measure's instrument (SM:435). The surviving product-side gaps are AC-169's patch-id mechanism (AC:2310, design:696; reconcile is Step 6) and the merge-queue merge (AC-196/197, Phase 2 per design:1791, though RUNBOOK:1863 puts AC-160–199 in Step 6). The list-not-rule ambiguity stands on those two.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed: no known-issues row mentions patch-id, merge ownership or a rule-vs-list framing (ARCH-10.3-006 and ARCH-8.10-004 restate the list). P2 is right: reconcile (AC-167..170) is Step 6 code and the wrapper's scope should be a principle before it is built; no Step-5 impact.
rows.corrected_statement: ADR-0077's read/write split is an enumerated list, not a rule: AC-169's patch-id computation (a reconcile read op gix does not expose as such) and the merge queue's merge/ref update (AC-196/197) have no assigned owner, and the forbids block does not forbid gix for a merge. `git worktree prune`, `cat-file -e` and `rev-list --count` are test/instrument invocations, not product ops, and do not need an owner.

rows.title: Review clone stays on gix, contradicting ADR-0077's claim that the hybrid moves gix away from the checkout surface

anchors.quote: - **shallow clone by SHA** for review checkouts;
- gix's exposure narrows to read operations, away from `gix-worktree-state` checkout and `gix-worktree` path handling, where its advisories cluster (0084).
| RUSTSEC-2025-0001 | `gix-worktree-state` | checkout sets files world-writable | ≥ 0.17.0 |

rows.statement: A shallow clone that produces a working tree the reviewer runs `repro.command` inside (AC-194) is a checkout performed by `gix-worktree-state` — the exact sub-crate whose advisory (RUSTSEC-2025-0001, files world-writable) the ADR cites as the surface the hybrid 'happens to avoid'. Labelling the clone a read-path op does not change what it writes to disk. The decision's stated positive consequence is therefore not delivered for the review clone, and neither S-GIX arm exercises clone.
rows.why_before_step5: No build blocker (the pin is clean as of 2026-09-08), but the ADR's rationale is the thing a future reader will use to decide whether a gix bump or a new advisory matters; as written it under-states gix's write exposure.
rows.remediation: Successor record: reclassify the review clone as a gix WRITE op that is retained deliberately (typed shallow-by-SHA clone is the benefit), strike or qualify the 'narrows away from checkout' consequence, and add clone to the list of ops ADR-0084's audit job and the Windows CI target specifically cover.

Neither S-GIX arm exercises clone (ADR-0077:78-79). Not a disclosed choice: no text qualifies the clone as a checkout.

rows.title: Checkpoint 6 greps cannot discriminate: wrapper-uniqueness grep misses ordinary imports; S-GIX verdict grep counts lines with 'go'

anchors.quote: grep -rn 'std::process::Command' crates/ --include=*.rs \
grep -cE 'S-GIX/(a|b).*(go|no-go)' references/adr/0091-*.md               # → 2: a verdict for EACH arm

rows.statement: [measured] A file containing `use std::process::{Command, Stdio}; Command::new("git")` and a file using `tokio::process::Command::new("git")` both yield 0 for the first grep, so 'one wrapper, one file' passes on a violation; and ADR-0077 forbids only `std::process::Command`, leaving tokio's spawn (which rk-adapter-claude lifts from the async spike runner) outside the letter of the rule. The second grep counts lines, matches 'go' as a substring (`algorithm`, `gone`) and `no-go` is subsumed by `go`: a record with both verdicts on one line plus one forbids line returns exactly 2, while ADR-0077 itself returns 1 from a forbids line with no verdict. Neither instrument decides what the checkpoint says it decides. Design §3 already uses clippy `disallowed_types` for the analogous rule (AC-003).

rows.remediation: Replace the first grep with a clippy `disallowed_types` entry for `std::process::Command` and `tokio::process::Command` scoped to all crates but rk-git's wrapper module; replace the second with a check of two explicit lines `S-GIX/a: go|no-go` and `S-GIX/b: go|no-go` (`grep -cE '^S-GIX/[ab]: (go|no-go)$'`).

rows.statement: Computed Wilson 95% intervals: 3/3 = [0.439, 1.000] and 0/3 = [0.000, 0.561] — they overlap on [0.439, 0.561], so at n=3 no pair of cells can fail METHOD-P §4.4(1)'s overlap test; the criterion had zero power, not 'almost none', and F37's 'can detect only an effect that is total' is arithmetically false (the §0.1/RUNBOOK phrase 'every Wilson interval overlaps by construction' is the correct one). In the other direction, at n=10 the 0/10 interval [0, 0.278] overlaps 1/10 [0.018, 0.404] and 3/10 [0.108, 0.603]; only >=6/10 vs 0/10 separates. A '1-in-10 effect' is therefore not resolvable at n=10 under the same per-item overlap criterion; the registered S-P7B design ('n = 10 per cell') repeats the powerless-at-its-own-n defect RB-GC-010 counts four instances of.

rows.title: `escalate` expiry opens another deadline-bearing gate; nothing bounds escalate-to-escalate chains, so no-hang is hollow

anchors.quote: THEN the escalation is itself a kernel-owned `Gate:` mark with its own (token, tree_hash, deadline) — not an in-activity
Every gate past its deadline is, after `reconcile()`, in exactly one of `fail`, `escalate` or `auto-decide`; the set of gates simultaneously past-deadline and open is empty
- Forbids a gate with no terminal path — an expiry must resolve to fail, escalate, or auto-decide, never leave the gate hanging.

rows.statement: AC-259 makes an expired gate with policy `escalate` open a second gate carrying its own deadline and (by AC-260/AC-276) its own per-class expiry action. No AC, design sentence or ADR says what class the escalation gate belongs to or bounds the chain; AC-256's doctor rule ('no gate both past-deadline and open') is satisfied at every step of an infinite escalate→escalate→… chain. Two implementers: A gives escalation gates a class whose policy is linted to be fail/auto-decide (or caps depth); B reuses the originating class and re-opens forever — which is the 'never a hang' failure ADR-0017 forbids, in slow motion.
rows.why_before_step5: The expiry state machine (AC-256's exhaustive test over expiry policy × arrival ordering) needs the escalation gate's class and a termination bound to be enumerable; without them the 'exhaustive' test has an unbounded state space and the policy-table lint (AC-260) cannot refuse a self-escalating class.
rows.remediation: Add one sentence to design §6.3.4 and a clause to AC-259 (or a new AC): an escalation gate's class is fixed (e.g. `escalation`) and the policy-table lint refuses `escalate` as that class's expiry action, so every chain terminates in fail or auto-decide within one hop; include a must-fail fixture row in AC-260's lint test.
rows.owner: Claude (AC/design edit); Ryan (AC-276 chooses the escalation class's terminal action)
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. AC-259:3303-3306 makes an escalate-expiry open a second Gate: mark with its own deadline; AC-260:3311-3318 requires every class to declare an expiry action; AC-276:3503-3511 leaves the per-class choice to a human; design:875-880, :1037 and ADR-0017:42/51 speak only of a terminal path per expiry. Grep across references/, RUNBOOK and spikes for an escalation gate's class, chain depth or bound returns nothing [measured]. Ambiguity real and undisclosed. Minor overstatement: AC-256's exhaustive test is over one gate's (policy x ordering) and is bounded regardless.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed: known-issues rows on escalation (ARCH-6.6-003, ADR-0017-FORB-50, ADR-0087-FORB-72, F33-LIM-019) record the terminal-path rule and activity-terminal ban, none the escalation gate's class or chain bound; not in anomaly_pool. P2 sound: an unspecified kernel behaviour that AC-276's pending human decision does not cover (it chooses per existing class; the escalation gate's class is undefined), fixable by one sentence and a lint fixture.

rows.title: 'Tree the human saw' undefined for an empty trailer commit over a dirty worktree; AC-254's 'commits between tree hashes' undefined

anchors.quote: THEN the recorded `tree_hash` is the hash of that same tree object, not of HEAD's commit, not of the index at a later
**git first**: trailers on a checkpoint commit, or an **empty commit** carrying the trailer when no checkpoint is due
`git worktree add` / `git worktree remove`; `git interpret-trailers --in-place` and/or `git commit --trailer` for **every** trailer write
THEN it names the commits and the changed paths between the recorded tree hash and the current one, and is byte-identical

rows.statement: Opening a gate writes a `Gate:` trailer on 'a checkpoint commit, or an empty commit' (design §5). On the empty-commit path the worktree may be dirty; AC-245 then requires a tree hash that is neither HEAD's tree nor a later index, and its instrument is 'a property test over dirty-worktree fixtures' — but no document says how a tree object is derived from a dirty worktree (untracked and ignored files in or out; temp-index write-tree vs in-memory hashing), and the git-exec write-side operation list at line 744 contains nothing that would produce one. AC-254 then requires the drift attachment to 'name the commits … between the recorded tree hash and the current one', which is undefined when the recorded tree is not the tree of any commit. Two implementers: A hashes HEAD's tree whenever the trailer commit is empty (violating AC-245's letter); B synthesises a tree from tracked+modified files (untracked excluded) and reports 'commits between' as commits since the trailer commit.
rows.why_before_step5: The drift predicate (AC-249/AC-253) and the void/re-open path are Phase-1 kernel behaviour; the two readings produce different void rates on the same repository, which is exactly the quantity SM-075 is meant to track.
rows.remediation: Add to design §6.3.2 (and AC-245's THEN) a definition: the recorded tree is the tree object of the trailer commit when the open is a checkpoint, and otherwise a tree written from the current index plus tracked modifications (state whether untracked files are included) via the git-exec wrapper (`git write-tree` on a temporary index — add it to the line-744 write-side list); restate AC-254 as 'commits since the trailer commit, and paths differing between the two trees'.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. AC-245:3150-3157 requires a tree object 'not of HEAD's commit, not of the index at a later instant' plus a property test over dirty-worktree fixtures; design §6.3.2 (:833-858) argues why a tree hash beats a SHA but never says how the tree object is produced; design:744's write-side list has no write-tree; AC-254:3259 asks for 'commits ... between' two trees. Grep for write-tree/dirty/untracked across design, ADR-0017 and spikes/runner/src finds no derivation rule; fingerprint.rs only digests git status. Both readings and the AC-254 gap follow.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed: the only dirty-tree row in known-issues is ARCH-1.2-043 (corpus provenance), unrelated; nothing in anomaly_pool. P2 sound: a Phase-1 kernel definition gap that changes the void rate SM-075 tracks, with a clear remediation and no evidence that Step 5 would build the wrong thing.

rows.title: ADR-0087 title/clause 3/forbids assert 'costs less' unconditionally, contra the design's own rule and 'safe under either answer'

anchors.quote: title: A mid-graph gate resumes into the same step, and costs less than a stage gate
3. Gate placement is therefore a value decision, not a cost decision: a mid-graph gate is not to be avoided on the grounds that it is dearer than a stage gate. Measured, it is cheaper.
**What would change this decision.** Any of: a lost or changed step output on a state holding more than one step; a resume cost above 1.5× F28's ~18.6k on the unrun 65-minute or 24-hour arms
"Mid-graph gates are cheaper than stage gates" may not be written without n=3 and the missing baseline named in the same sentence.
The decision below is taken because it is safe under *either* answer, not because this measurement lic

rows.statement: Design §6.3.6, §0.1 row 29 and §7.10 rule that 'cheaper than a stage gate' may not be stated without n=3 and the missing baseline in the same sentence, and that the decision is 'safe under either answer'. The accepted ADR that governs the row states the forbidden sentence in its title (restated wherever the ADR is listed by title), in Decision clause 3 and in its forbids block with no qualifier, and its 'what would change this decision' names a >1.5x cost result — i.e. the decision is not safe under either answer per the ADR, while METHOD-P §5.4's registered consequence of that kill was only a pricing/`mandatory`-default change, not withdrawal of resume-into-same-step.
rows.why_before_step5: Pack authors and the AC-273 placement-record lint take their rule from the ADR's forbids block; today that block forbids a placement argument on evidence the design itself says may not be stated that way (and, per G08-01, on a cross-class ratio). No build step is blocked; the record is inconsistent with its own governing design text.
rows.remediation: Supersede ADR-0087 (never edit): new record keeps clauses 1-2 and 4-6, drops 'costs less' from the title and clause 3, rewrites the forbids line as 'forbids deriving placement from a cost model', and scopes 'what would change this decision' so a >1.5x result changes the pricing guidance (per METHOD-P §5.4) rather than the suspend/resume shape; mark ADR-0087 superseded_by accordingly.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. ADR-0087 title (:3), clause 3 (:48) and forbids line (:76) assert 'costs less' with no n=3/missing-baseline qualifier in the sentence; design:900 forbids exactly that; design:894 says the decision is safe under either answer. Further, ADR-0087:17 says the >1.5x kill would make escalation 'activity-terminal', whereas METHOD-P §5.4:229-230 attaches activity-terminal to the lost-output kill and only a pricing change to the cost kill — so 'what would change this decision' (:56) rests on a misattributed consequence. Confirmed, slightly stronger than stated.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed: ADR-0087-FORB-75 records the forbids clause as a deliberate exception and ARCH-1.2-040 records the design's 'may not be written without n=3' rule; neither records that the accepted ADR violates that rule in its title/clause 3/forbids, nor the misattributed kill consequence at ADR-0087:17. P2 sound: no build step depends on the sentence; AC-273's placement lint reads the forbids block, so the record inconsistency has a downstream consumer but is not blocking.

rows.title: 'F28 proves a keep-warm dispatch buys nothing' is not what F28 measured; its correction credits other dispatching for the warm 48%

anchors.quote: so "keep the cache warm" suggests itself. F28 proves it buys nothing: **18,6
A "keep the cache warm" optimisation is the tempting wrong answer, and F28 [measured] proves it buys nothing:
**F28 proves such a dispatch buys nothing;** this metric is what would catch someone adding it.
directory-independent, and which this programme's own constant unrelated

rows.statement: F28 ran no keep-alive arm. Its H1 table shows an in-TTL re-read is free (0.9 min: share 1.000, creation 0) and its correction says the 48% that survived 49.7 h did so because 'this programme's own constant unrelated dispatching kept [it] perpetually warm' — i.e. dispatching does keep prefix warm. What F28 establishes is that the rewrite is bounded (~18.6k, or ~29.7k under a card prompt), which makes a keep-alive unnecessary and, for long gates, a net loss; it does not prove it 'buys nothing'. The real ground for AC-243/SM-077 is F22's mark-not-process rule, which the same rows already cite.
rows.why_before_step5: None for the build; AC-243's negative criterion stands on AC-240/F22 regardless. A characterisation cited as [measured, F28] that the finding does not contain.
rows.remediation: Reword the three anchors to 'F28 bounds what it could buy at one prefix rewrite (18.6k-29.7k) per gate, so it is not worth a process; F22 forbids the process anyway'.
rows.truth_reason: All four anchors verbatim [measured]. F28's H1 table (FINDINGS:1711-1716) shows share 1.000/creation 0 at 0.9 min and 18,603 at 65 min and 49.7 h; no keep-alive arm exists in METHOD-H or the h1*.jsonl files [measured]. The correction (FINDINGS:1800-1805) attributes the surviving 48% to 'this programme's own constant unrelated dispatching' and :1815 says the default prompt 'rides the shared segment other work keeps warm' — i.e. dispatching does keep prefix warm. 'Proves it buys nothing' is therefore an over-reading of a bounded-cost result; the finder's characterisation is accurate.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed: no known-issues row contains 'keep the cache warm', 'buys nothing' or 'perpetually warm'; not in anomaly_pool. P3 sound: AC-243's negative criterion stands on F22/AC-240 regardless, so the only harm is a [measured] tag on a claim F28 does not contain, restated in three documents — hygiene of the corpus's own evidence discipline, worth the reword.

rows.title: Unverifiable is a computed EvidenceClass variant in three places and not in the closed enum AC-284 defines

anchors.quote: `narrowed-pin` iff only the discriminating assertion flips; `advisory` in every remaining case, including every
closed `EvidenceClass` enum (no `_ =>` fallthrough to a blocking class); a fuzz input that produces `advisory`, never a panic.
| `advisory` / `Unverifiable` | Never blocks | Never blocks | ADR-0074 clauses 4–5 [documented] |
- **Instrument:** `finding` records with `class = Unverifiable`, split by reason (`both_fail` | `cannot_run` | `timeout`).
block set; a doctor rule that **every finding classed `reproduced` or `mutation-survived` carries either a re-execution
GIVEN the same repro record and re-execution record

rows.statement: AC-284 defines the computed class as a closed four-value table (reproduced | mutation-survived | narrowed-pin | advisory, 'advisory in every remaining case'), but the design's policy table lists `Unverifiable` as a fifth 'Computed class' row, SM-088 instruments `class = Unverifiable`, SM-096 writes `Unverifiable{timeout}`, and AC-290's doctor rule speaks of a finding 'classed reproduced' that carries an Unverifiable reason - i.e. class and Unverifiable coexist on one finding. A second, coupled ambiguity: AC-284/AC-286 take the re-execution record as a classifier INPUT ('GIVEN the same repro record and re-execution record'), while AC-287/AC-290 assume a finding can be classed `reproduced` before any re-execution record exists.
rows.why_before_step5: Step 5.3 snapshots the golden schema for `Findings` and Step 7b builds the classifier and the `review_block`/`finding` telemetry. Engineer A ships `enum EvidenceClass {Reproduced, MutationSurvived, NarrowedPin, Advisory}` plus a separate `Disposition::Unverifiable(reason)` set after re-execution; Engineer B ships a five-variant enum recomputed from the re-execution record, under which AC-287's 'classed reproduced with no re-execution record' state is unreachable and AC-290's doctor rule is vacuous. The two produce different golden schemas, different SM-085/SM-088 field semantics, and different doctor rules.
rows.remediation: Amend the AC register (AC-284 or a note under §9.2) to state which of the two shapes is binding: (a) EvidenceClass is the four-variant closed enum computed from the model's repro record alone, and `Unverifiable{reason}` is a re-execution OUTCOME carried beside the class (then fix SM-088's 'class = Unverifiable' to 'outcome = Unverifiable' and the design policy-table row label); or (b) EvidenceClass has five variants and is computed after re-execution (then rewrite AC-287/AC-290 so they do not presuppose a `reproduced` class without a re-execution record). Say in the same note whether the model's advisory `evidence` label may take the value `Unverifiable`.
rows.owner: design author (AC register §9 + design §6.4.2); implementer must not choose silently
rows.truth_reason: All six anchors verbatim [measured]. Drift is real: SM-088:656 'class = Unverifiable' vs SM-104:762 'outcome = Unverifiable(timeout)'; design:932 lists Unverifiable under 'Computed class'; AC-286:3628 names the re-execution record as classifier input where design:915 and ADR-0074 clause 2 (:53) compute from the repro record. But 'two equally readable shapes' is overstated: ADR-0074 clauses 2-5 settle it (four-valued class from the repro record; clause 4 makes Unverifiable a re-execution outcome that 'is advisory'), and AC-287:3641 / AC-290 fit that. Wording alignment, not a blocking ambiguity.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed: known-issues.json has no row on EvidenceClass, AC-284, AC-290 or the class/outcome split (only ADR-0074-FORB-84 and SM-5.1-032, which record other facts about Unverifiable); anomaly_pool has none. Nearest recorded item is AC-15.3-001 (§9 cites ADR-0004 instead of ADR-0074), the route by which an implementer could miss the settling clauses. P1 is inflated: the binding AC-284 text and ADR-0074 both give the four-variant enum, so Step 7b would not build the wrong classifier; the residue is a telemetry field name (SM-088) and three loose sentences. P2.
rows.corrected_statement: `Unverifiable` is written as a computed class in three places (SM-088 instrument 'class = Unverifiable'; design §6.4.2's 'Computed class' column; AC-306/ADR-0074 clause 5 'its class blocks... false for advisory and Unverifiable') and as a re-execution outcome elsewhere (AC-287, AC-290, SM-104 'outcome = Unverifiable(timeout)'); AC-286 also names the re-execution record as a classifier input where ADR-0074 clause 2 and design §6.4.1 row 2 compute the class from the repro record alone. ADR-0074 clauses 2-5 fix the shape (four-variant EvidenceClass; Unverifiable is a re-execution outcome that never blocks); the AC/SM/design wording should be aligned to it and SM-088's instrument field renamed.

rows.statement: RUNBOOK 7c lists AC-280–AC-319 as the Phase-1 acceptance set, which includes AC-312 (a release regression corpus with negative-control and seeded fixtures, verified by a corpus regression job). ADR-0074 forbids 'shipping the fixture family without the "presented as already approved" arm'. That arm (S-SUBTLE-CB) is registered, unrun, unsized and unpriced, is marked 'gates Phase 1? **Filled by the model at Ryan's direction, 2026-09-04. NOT BLIND.**

rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. design:956 reads 'severity is Ryan's, one operator, blind'; design:1049 reads 'severity adjudicated 2026-09-04, NOT BLIND (filled by the model at Ryan's direction; kappa forfeited...)'; :31, :123, :1873 and RUNBOOK:881 ('That sheet is NOT BLIND at all, by its own header') agree; the sheet header (e3-severity-annotation-ryan.md:3) says NOT BLIND. rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed: ARCH-6.6-012 (design:1049) records NOT BLIND; no row anchors design:956 or the word 'blind' as a claim [measured, search_index]. rows.title: ADR-0082 and ADR-0088 credit F24 with '≥13 of 23 (57%)'; F24 established ≥5/23 (22%) and the 13 is F31's

anchors.quote: - [measured] F24: CLEAN's ground truth is wrong for **at least 13 of 23 items (57%)** — every item shipped and was approved, and the defects
and F24 established its ground truth is wrong for at least 13 of 23 items (57%) — the defects were there and the human process approved the
F24 established CLEAN's ground truth is wrong for at least 13 of 23 items (57%), so every rate measured against it is provisional.
to be wrong for at least five of 23 items (22%).** Any false-positive rate
and it is now known wrong for at least 13 of 23 items rather than 5.
Wrong for **≥13 of 23 = 57%** (brief §E); the E3 adjudication established **≥5/23 = 22%** at the time it was run.

rows.statement: Two accepted ADRs (0088 at lines 21, 59 and 94 - the last tagged [measured]; 0082 at line 93) attribute the ≥13/23 (57%) CLEAN mislabel figure to F24. F24's own text establishes 'at least five of 23 items (22%)'; the raise to 13 comes from F31's S-TYPED adjudication (F31-DRAFT line 91), and the design's §1.2 row 122 gets the attribution right. The ADRs' evidence sections therefore cite a finding for a number it does not contain.
rows.why_before_step5: No build impact; ADR evidence sections are the immutable record, and ADR-0088's [measured] tag on a wrong F-number is the kind of provenance slip the corpus's own §10.x review calls out as its characteristic failure mode.
rows.remediation: Per the house rule ADRs are not edited: record an erratum in references/adr/README.md (or a corrigendum note the design §10.x review carries) stating that in ADR-0082:93 and ADR-0088:21/59/94 'F24' should read 'F24 (≥5/23) raised to ≥13/23 by F31'. If a superseding record for 0088 is ever cut, carry the correct attribution.
rows.truth_reason: All six anchors verbatim [measured]. F24 (FINDINGS.md:1350) says 'at least five of 23 items (22%)'; the evidence brief's F24 row (:39) says '>=5/23 = 22%'; the raise to 13 first appears in F31-DRAFT.md:91 ('now known wrong for at least 13 of 23 items rather than 5'); design:122 attributes it correctly. ADR-0088 attributes >=13/23 to F24 at :21, :59 ('>=13/23 by F24') and :94 (tagged [measured]); ADR-0082:93 does the same. Both ADRs list F31-DRAFT among their sources, so the correct finding was available when they were cut.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed: the known-issues row on the 13/23 figure (ARCH-1.2-030) and the anomaly_pool constant-variant row clean.13of23 (>=12 vs >=13) concern the value, not its attribution to F24; no row anchors ADR-0082:93 or ADR-0088:21/59/94 for this [measured]. P2 correct: an evidence-section provenance slip in two accepted ADRs, no build consequence; the house rule that ADRs are not edited makes the erratum route the right remediation.

is what would buy κ back, which is why E3-SEV stays named as the open route.

rows.statement: The §10.5 register defines E3-SEV as 'what a blind annotation of the preserved BLANK would still buy' and in the same row marks it DONE on the strength of the non-blind sheet; §0.1 row 31 says 'E3-SEV stays named as the open route'. One id carries two statuses, and RUNBOOK 3c's checkpoint (grep E3-SEV -> 'DONE') passes whichever is meant.
rows.why_before_step5: None; exit (d) is discharged either way and the RUNBOOK already records the split. It is a register-hygiene defect: the discharge rule of ADR-0012 keys on a row's status, and this row's status is not single-valued.
rows.remediation: Split the row: mark E3-SEV DONE (non-blind, 2026-09-04 sheet) and register the blind re-annotation under a new id (e.g. E3-SEV-BLIND, consumer SM-086, cost $0 + Ryan's time, status 'Registered, not taken'), and change §0.1 row 31 to name the new id as the open route.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. design:1873 in one row defines E3-SEV as 'what a blind annotation of the preserved e3-severity-annotation-BLANK.md would still buy' and sets Status 'DONE - e3-severity-annotation-ryan.md' (the sheet it has just called NOT BLIND); design:31 says 'E3-SEV stays named as the open route'. RUNBOOK:881 discloses the split ('the E3 half discharges (d)'s result, not (d)'s blindness') and :908 greps the id for 'DONE', so the two-valued status is known and worked around, but the id is not split.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed: ARCH-10.5-014 records the row verbatim (definition and DONE together) without flagging the two statuses; no row anchors design:31's 'open route' sentence for this [measured]. P3 is right: exit (d) is discharged either way and RUNBOOK 3c records the split; the value is a single-valued status for an ADR-0012 discharge-by-id grep. Retains remediation value (split the id), so not immaterial.

rows.title: S-SUBTLE-CB's register row carries no cost, and the §0.1 row that gates the area never names the spike id

anchors.quote: | SM-092, SM-093; ADR-0088 | Paired per item; must be **sized before it runs** — at n=5 with detection at ceiling only a large effect is observable | No | Registered, unrun |
`S-GIX`, `S-TTL1`, `S-H1c`, `S-SUBTLE-CB`, `S-CODEX`, `S-RETRY`. §10.5 carries all of them with cost and gate
| The S-SUBTLE "presented as already approved" arm, paired per item, sized before it runs (at n=5 with detection at ceiling only a large effect is observable) |

rows.statement: The §10.5 register's Cost column for S-SUBTLE-CB holds sizing prose and no figure - not even the 'Unpriced' that S-H1c and S-FANOUT use - while the 2026-09-10 handoff asserts '§10.5 carries all of them with cost and gate'. ADR-0088 itself supplies the priceable inputs (paired draws over n=5 at a 1,071 s median; S-VAR's 60 draws cost $176.96 / 16.2 h). §0.1 row 30's 'What unblocks it' cell describes the arm but never names S-SUBTLE-CB, so the id is defined and cited only inside §10 (ids.json: 6 citations, all §10 or the handoff), and the row's ADR-0012 discharge cannot be grepped by id.
rows.why_before_step5: None; the arm does not gate Phase 1. Hygiene of the register ADR-0012 makes load-bearing.
rows.remediation: Put a figure or 'Unpriced' in the Cost cell (a first-order estimate: 2 framings x 5 items x k draws at S-TYPED's median $3.03/review), name S-SUBTLE-CB in §0.1 row 30's 'What unblocks it' cell, and correct the handoff's 'with cost' claim or the row.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. The Cost cell holds sizing prose and no figure; S-CASCADE:1885 copies it; S-H1c:1867 and S-FANOUT:1875 use 'Unpriced' [measured, column parse of :1858-1894]. But it is not an omission: ADR-0088 clauses 5-6 and design:969 require the arm to be 'sized before it is run' or report a bound, so 'must be sized before it runs' is the disclosed reason no price exists - a deliberate, recorded choice. The handoff's 'with cost' (:71) is loose at most. §0.1 row 30 not naming the id is true and hygiene only; the id appears at design :1832, :1874, :1885, :1914 [measured].
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN, not NEW: ARCH-10.5-015 records the row verbatim including its Cost cell; H10-LOOP-P-004 records the handoff sentence. Neither flags the token/id gap. P3 is correct and marginal: the remediation is two cell edits, with grep-ability under ADR-0012 as the only value. Kept WEAKENED rather than REFUTED because a discharge grep by id on §0.1 row 30 would currently miss.
rows.corrected_statement: S-SUBTLE-CB's §10.5 Cost cell (design:1874) states a sizing precondition instead of a figure or the register's 'Unpriced' token, and §0.1 row 30 (design:30) describes the arm without naming the spike id; the handoff (:71) says §10.5 carries the spike 'with cost'. The absence of a price is the disclosed consequence of ADR-0088 clauses 5-6 (sized before it runs); the residual defect is the missing token and the unnamed id.

rows.title: RUNBOOK Step 7a names AC-480–AC-519 whole as its Phase-1 acceptance set, including unbuildable CONDITIONAL and Phase-2/3 rows

anchors.quote: **Acceptance set: AC-480–AC-519** (ports, fakes; AC-239/AC-496/AC-502 are out of scope — S-CODEX is unrun and
Five named ports — event store, harness, tracker, docs site, toolchain — each a **sync** trait with one real
them as settled requirements on a build runbook is the exact failure this subsection exists to prevent.

- The whole surviving distribution block (AC-512, AC-514..AC-517, AC-519's receipt/rename halves, SM-149) is UNBUILDABLE until §4.9 is reopened and a distribution mechanism is actually decided. A reader who skims past the CONDITIONAL banner will read them as requirements.
Note: `rk-plugin-gen` is a **Phase 2** deliverable (§7); nothing in this sub-section is checkable before then.

Phase 1 ships exactly one adapter behind each port it uses — SQLite, Claude Code and Node — and **no tracker and no docs-site adapter at all**; GitHub and mdBook are Phase 3 (SM-148, corrected against proposal §7).

rows.statement: Step 7a's acceptance set is the entire ports-dist range minus three ids, so it binds Phase 1 to AC-501..AC-506 (rk-plugin-gen, Phase 2, 'nothing checkable before then'), AC-507/508/510 (GitHub and mdBook adapters, Phase 3), the six CONDITIONAL installer criteria the register calls UNBUILDABLE, and retired AC-513 [measured]. The exclusion reason given for AC-502 (S-CODEX) is wrong — AC-502 is dialect parity in the generator; its siblings AC-501/503-506 are equally out of scope and are not excluded. Line 1877 compounds this by describing all five ports as shipping 'one real adapter' in a Phase-1 step, against design line 246.
rows.why_before_step5: The runbook says the design governs where they disagree, and the design says reading the CONDITIONAL rows as runbook requirements is 'the exact failure this subsection exists to prevent'; the runbook does exactly that. As written, Step 7a can never be signed off against its own acceptance set (fifteen of the 36 named criteria are Phase 2/3 or unbuildable), and an implementer taking line 1877 literally builds two adapters Phase 1 does not ship. Checkpoint 7a's four commands are unaffected, which is why this is P1 not P0.
rows.remediation: Amend RUNBOOK Step 7a's acceptance set to the Phase-1 subset: AC-480..AC-495, AC-497..AC-500, AC-511, AC-509, AC-518, and AC-499 only for ports with a Phase-1 real adapter (see G10-02); list AC-501..AC-506 as Phase 2, AC-507/508/510 as Phase 3, AC-512/514..517/519(part) as CONDITIONAL-unbuildable, AC-496 as PROVISIONAL, AC-482 as human-gated; correct the AC-502 exclusion reason; reword line 1877 to 'each a sync trait with a fake, and a real adapter where Phase 1 ships one (SQLite, Claude, Node)'.
rows.truth_reason: All six anchors verbatim [measured]. Core holds: Step 7a names AC-480–AC-519 whole; its five sibling sets (RUNBOOK:1774, 1863, 2006, 2118) carve out non-evaluable rows and RUNBOOK never mentions CONDITIONAL, rk-plugin-gen or distribution [measured]. Two sub-claims fail: (a) AC-502's exclusion is NOT wrong — AC:185 says 'AC-502's dialect-parity domain is undefined until [S-CODEX]'; (b) line 1877's 'one real adapter' is the port rule as design:1852 restates it ('Both ports ship with a fake and one real adapter'), not a Phase-1 claim. Count off by one: 37 named ids, not 36.
rows.material_reason: NEW → SHARPENS-KNOWN: the corpus records the phasing at AC:6373 ('roughly half the area is unexercisable during Phase 1: rk-plugin-gen (AC-501..AC-506) is Phase 2, the GitHub and mdBook adapters (AC-507, AC-508, AC-510) are Phase 3') and the skim-past-banner hazard at AC:6366 — unindexed in known-issues.json but in the corpus. New is that the RUNBOOK does what AC:6366/design:1589 warn against. P1 → P2: no Phase-1 crate is blocked; Checkpoint 7a's commands gate the step, RUNBOOK:5 excludes Phases 2–4, the register's banners fence the rows. Wrong record, not wrong build.
rows.corrected_statement: RUNBOOK Step 7a's acceptance set (RUNBOOK:1902) names AC-480–AC-519 whole, unlike its five sibling steps which carve out non-evaluable rows. It therefore binds a Phase-1 sign-off to AC-501/503–506 (rk-plugin-gen, Phase 2 — AC:6194), AC-507/508/510 (Phase 3), the CONDITIONAL AC-512/514–517 and part of AC-519 (AC:6276–6280, 6366), and retired AC-513 — fourteen of thirty-seven named ids [measured]. The AC-502 exclusion on S-CODEX grounds is correct (AC:185). Line 1877 restates the proposal's port rule and matches design:1852; imprecise in a Phase-1 step, not a contradiction of design:246.

rows.title: AC-499 requires the real Claude adapter in a CI matrix, a decision ADR-0010 punts past Phase 1; two ports have no real adapter in Phase 1

anchors.quote: *Verified by:* one parameterised conformance suite per port, instantiated over `{fake, real}`; a CI matrix row per instantiation.
- Decisions about CI execution of the Claude adapter may not be made under this ADR; it is explicitly punted to Phase 3 or later.
"CI is a Phase 3+ question": no decision is taken here about how (or whether) the Claude adapter runs under CI; that is explicitly left open past Phase 1.

- AC-499's conformance matrix runs the shared suite against the REAL Claude adapter, implying model dispatches in CI at unbudgeted cost, and sits in tension with AC-498's network-denied isolation job. Nothing bounds that cost and no measure tracks it.

rows.statement: The register records AC-499's cost and its tension with AC-498, but not that its named instrument requires the subscription-only Claude adapter to run under CI — the one question ADR-0010 explicitly leaves open past Phase 1 [documented]. Separately, in Phase 1 the Tracker and DocsSite ports have no real adapter (design:246), so the `{fake, real}` matrix cannot be instantiated for two of five ports, and the AC carries no phase caveat [inferred from design:246 and proposal §7].
rows.why_before_step5: AC-499 sits inside Step 7a's acceptance set (G10-01) and is marked binding. An implementer either wires a CI job that needs a Claude subscription session (no path exists — ADR-0010 line 41) or quietly drops the real row and reports the suite green on fakes only, which is the vacuity SM-151 warns about. Neither outcome is what the criterion says. No first-line code is wrong because of it; the record is.
rows.remediation: Amend AC-499 with a phase clause: in Phase 1 the matrix instantiates `{fake, real}` for EventStore (SQLite) and Toolchain (Node) only; the Harness real row is deferred to the CI decision ADR-0010 punts (record it as a named open item with a consumer, per ADR-0012), and Tracker/DocsSite real rows arrive with Phase 3. Note the dependency in the §14 State line.
rows.truth_reason: All four anchors verbatim [measured]. First half holds: AC-499's instrument ('a CI matrix row per instantiation' over {fake, real}) needs the real Claude adapter under CI, which ADR-0010:32/46 leaves undecided past Phase 1 [documented]. Second half is defused by text the finder missed: AC-499's GIVEN is 'a port with a fake and a real adapter' (AC:6171), so for Tracker/DocsSite in Phase 1 the criterion is vacuously unmet, not unsatisfiable — the AC carries its own phase conditioning. 'Cannot be instantiated' should read 'is not instantiated'.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed: rows ADR-0010-NEG-40 and ADR-0010-FORB-45 record the CI gap, and AC:6369 (unindexed) records AC-499's real-Claude CI cost; no row joins the two. P2 is right: the Harness matrix row is unbuildable as specified but nothing in Step 7a/7c is blocked (fake rows and SQLite/Node real rows run), and SM-151 already discloses saturation.
rows.corrected_statement: AC-499's named instrument (a CI matrix row per {fake, real} instantiation, AC:6175) requires the real Claude adapter to run under CI, which ADR-0010 (:32, :46) declines to decide before Phase 3+ and whose Negative consequence (:41) says no path exists. AC:6369 records the cost and the AC-498 tension but not this dependency on an undecided ADR. Tracker/DocsSite real rows are absent in Phase 1 by AC-499's own GIVEN clause — a vacuous pass, not a defect.

rows.title: Design carries the AC-511 id conflict as unresolved in five places; the register settles it, but reusing AC-511/512 breaches ADR-0085 rule 7

anchors.quote: Both statements are left standing. The sources do not settle which criterion holds the id, and ids are fixed and are never renumbered (ADR-0085)
| AC-511 | 'a compiled-in payload wins over a payload-shaped cwd' (cut: contradicts §4.9) | the `--bare` half split from AC-488 | ports-dist |
(Split from the former compound AC-488. Uses the id freed by the cut of the old AC-511; see Refutation notes.)
Ids are never reused within their scope.
- Forbids editing an accepted ADR; forbids a one-sided supersession link; forbids reusing a retired number.
- **§8.8's AC-511 id conflict is still unresolved**, and §3.6.1 now adds a third home for the same rule rather than settling it.

rows.statement: The AC register (binding on the runbook) states in §0.4 and in AC-511's own body that AC-511 is now the `--bare` half of AC-488, so the design's §8.4 and §2 citations of AC-511 as the `--bare`/API-key assertion are correct and the 'conflict' at design:1585, :357, :362, :1345 and :1969 does not exist [measured]. What does exist is unrecorded: the register re-issued AC-511 and AC-512 (and four other ids) after cutting them, which ADR-0085 rule 7 ('never reused within their scope') and its forbids block ('reusing a retired number') prohibit; the register distinguishes 'cut and freed' from 'retired' without any ADR licensing that distinction.
rows.why_before_step5: Low build impact: AC-511 as defined is the criterion the design and RUNBOOK 7c actually mean. The cost is operator time — the design tells the builder to re-read the area file before touching either statement, for a question the register already answers. The ADR-0085 breach matters for the convention the whole corpus relies on: if cut ids may be re-issued, every pre-refutation citation is suspect, which is exactly what §0.4 warns.
rows.remediation: Amend the design (dated amendment, not an edit of ADR-0085) to withdraw the five 'unresolved' notes, citing AC §0.4 line 122. Either supersede ADR-0085 partially with a record that licenses re-issue of a cut id under a §0.4-style hazard table, or record the six reuses as a tracked convention debt in ADR-0085's consumer/backfill note; do not renumber (ADR-0085).
rows.truth_reason: All six anchors verbatim; design lines 357, 362, 1345, 1585, 1969 each cite the AC-511 conflict as unresolved [measured]. The register settles it: §0.4 (AC:122) records AC-511 as 'the --bare half split from AC-488' and AC:6069 says 'Uses the id freed by the cut of the old AC-511', so 'the sources do not settle which criterion holds the id' is stale. The ADR-0085 tension is real: rule 7 (:74) 'Ids are never reused within their scope' and the forbids block bar reuse, yet §0.4 re-issues six cut ids and distinguishes 'retired' from 'reused' by its own fiat; no record licenses that.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed: ARCH-10.x-L-003 (design:1969) records the design's 'still unresolved' stance; AC-0.4-T-005 / AC-0.4-P-003 (AC:114, :122) record the reuse as a hazard; no row records that the two artefacts now disagree or that §0.4 contravenes ADR-0085 rule 7 as written. P2 correct: no build consequence (AC-511 as defined is what RUNBOOK 7c means), but five stale 're-read before changing' notes and an accepted-ADR/register contradiction are record defects.

rows.title: AC-504 cites ADR-0016 for the StructuredOutput rule; ADR-0016 does not carry it and no ADR does, though §0.1 says DECIDED, gates Phase 1

anchors.quote: brief §C5 ("forces `StructuredOutput` in every card whose role demands a schema, checked at configuration time") · decisions: ADR-0016, proposal §4.9
"`--system-prompt` = the card body (static)" for Phase 1; volatile input goes in the user message (stable prefix / volatile suffix).
| Structured output is a configuration-time check | **DECIDED** | An agent card's `tools` allowlist **silently disables `--json-schema`**

rows.statement: ADR-0016's body mentions no tool allowlist, no `--json-schema` and no `StructuredOutput` (grep: zero hits); it decides the card-delivery route and a TTL pin [measured]. AC-504 — and the three other homes of the same rule, AC-095, AC-205, AC-417 — nonetheless name ADR-0016 in `decisions:`. Only ADR-0084 (dependency policy) mentions StructuredOutput at all. §0.1 row 46 declares the rule DECIDED with '—' in the unblocks column and 'Yes' for gates-Phase-1: a Phase-1-gating rule with no decision record and four criteria pointing at the wrong one.
rows.why_before_step5: Nobody builds the wrong thing — F20 is unambiguous and RUNBOOK Checkpoint 7c tests `structured_output_required`. But ADR-0085 rule 8 makes the AC→ADR trace mandatory, and the trace here is false; a reader following AC-504 to its decision finds a record about prompt caching. The known-issues row records the missing artifact, not the mis-citation.
rows.remediation: Record the StructuredOutput configuration-time rule as an ADR of its own (evidence F20, consumers AC-095, AC-205, AC-417, AC-504, and the kernel/doctor rule tables), then amend the four criteria's `decisions:` fields and the §15 ADR-0016 consumer row; leave ADR-0016 untouched.
rows.owner: AC register maintainer; ADR author (Ryan Britton)
rows.truth_reason: All four anchors verbatim [measured]. grep over ADR-0016 for StructuredOutput/json-schema/allowlist: 0 hits; grep -il across references/adr/ for structured.output|structured_output|json.schema: only 0084-dependency-policy.md, which cites F20 as evidence, not decision [measured]. rows.title: SM-145 is saturated at zero by AC-503's construction and is not disclosed as such, unlike SM-148 and SM-151

anchors.quote: - **Instrument:** commits whose changed paths lie wholly inside generated trees, counted per 100 commits by a CI script.
- **Kill:** a re-sync rate at or above 7% means generation is not actually reproducible from source and the generator should emit fewer artifacts.
THEN the regenerated output is byte-identical to what is checked in

- The area has essentially no discriminating measure before Phase 2: SM-145/146/147/149/151 have no baseline, SM-148 and SM-151 are explicitly saturated, and SM-153/154 are the only two with measured priors.

rows.statement: A commit whose changed paths lie wholly inside generated trees is by definition a re-sync commit; AC-503 blocks any merge where the checked-in trees differ from regeneration, so on a tree where AC-503 gates, such commits cannot reach main and the instrument reads zero by construction [inferred from the two texts]. That is SATURATED in the corpus's own vocabulary, and the kill ('at or above 7%') can fire only if AC-503 is switched off. SM-145's header says 'no baseline; external comparator only'; the area's residual note lists only SM-148 and SM-151 as saturated.
rows.why_before_step5: None for Phase 1 (first measurement is 100 commits after rk-plugin-gen lands, Phase 2). Recorded because the corpus is careful to label saturated metrics and missed this one.
rows.remediation: Amend SM-145's header to 'saturated at zero while AC-503 gates; the discriminating quantity is the regeneration-diff failure count in CI', and adjust the kill to that count, mirroring SM-151's 'coverage growth is the real metric' treatment.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim, but the inference is wrong. AC-503 fails CI when checked-in trees differ from regeneration (AC:6206–6208). A commit wholly inside generated trees is the re-sync that RESTORES equality after a prior source-only commit — it passes AC-503 and reaches main; AC-503 blocks the stale source change, not the re-sync. So the instrument counts exactly the tax SM-145 names and is not zero by construction [inferred]. SM-145's Target already discloses the interaction ('AC-503's regeneration gate making a re-sync commit unnecessary rather than merely rare', SM:1050).
rows.material_reason: Refuted on truth, so no defect to classify. For completeness: the corpus records SM-145's no-baseline status (SM-NOBASE-085/086) and its AC-503 dependence (SM:1050); a saturation label the instrument's own logic does not support would sharpen nothing. P3 as filed; no remediation warranted.

rows.title: Idempotency key: three-part in every AC and the design, four-part `(run_id, activity_id, step_id, attempt)` in the schema

anchors.quote: THEN it cannot be constructed without an `(run_id, activity_id, attempt)` idempotency key, and a malformed key
`(run_id, activity_id, attempt)` is unique across the whole log.
| Every non-deterministic step is its own process with an idempotency key `(run_id, activity_id, step_id, attempt)` and a timeout with a number | proposal §4.2, L5.4/L5.6, H4 |

| **Idempotency** | `(run_id, activity_id, attempt)` | A dispatch cannot be constructed without it — the port takes it by value, not `Option`

rows.statement: Under ADR-0022 an activity is a graph whose agent/tool steps are each a harness dispatch with their own `retry = { max = N }`. AC-010/011/012 and design §3.5 key each dispatch by `(run_id, activity_id, attempt)`; the schema the ADR rests on keys it by `(run_id, activity_id, step_id, attempt)`. With the three-part key two agent steps of one pass share a key, so AC-011's 'unique across the whole log' assertion and AC-012's one-`activity_committed`-per-`(run_id, activity_id)` rule cannot both hold for a multi-step activity; P8's own records already label dispatches per step (`...#attempt`, `occurrence`). [measured]
rows.why_before_step5: Two implementers build different port signatures (`Harness::dispatch` takes a 3-tuple or a 4-tuple), different log-uniqueness invariants and different dedup semantics; AC-010's `trybuild` test pins whichever shape is chosen first. This is the kernel's first type.
rows.remediation: Amend AC-010..AC-012 and design §3.5 to the four-part key (or define `activity_id` as a step-activation id and say so), and state at which granularity `attempt` increments and `activity_committed` is emitted (per step activation under ADR-0022).
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured]. Grep over references/, adr/ and RUNBOOK: the four-part key appears only at activity-graph-schema.md:10; the three-part key at proposal:114, AC-010:294, AC-011:306, AC-508:6251, design:306/320. The schema row cites 'proposal §4.2' for the four-part key, but proposal:114 states the three-part one, so the schema added `step_id` while claiming to restate the proposal. Schema §4 (line 83) makes each agent/tool step a dispatch with its own `retry = { max = N }`, so AC-011's log-wide uniqueness over the triple is under-determined for multi-step activities.
rows.material_reason: NEW confirmed: search_index has no row for 'idempotency', and the anomaly_pool has none. P2 is right: the AC register is internally consistent on the three-part key, so 7b builds a definite shape; the defect is that the shape does not name the granularity at which `attempt` increments and `activity_committed` (AC-012:314) is emitted for a multi-step activity, and the schema disagrees — a record ambiguity with a design consequence, not a blocked workstream.
rows.corrected_statement: The schema's four-part key (activity-graph-schema.md:10) is attributed to proposal §4.2, which itself states the three-part `(run_id, activity_id, attempt)` key (proposal:114); the schema introduced `step_id` without saying so, and the AC register and design follow the proposal.

rows.title: cancel(handle) is a port operation the kernel can never call under blocking sync dispatch; Harness trait shape admits two designs
rows.known_issue_match: none (ARCH-10.4-030 covers the Windows handle leak, not the call shape)

anchors.quote: `dispatch(ActivitySpec) -> Result<Typed, StepError>`; capability registry with dated probes; cost/usage; **`cancel(handle)`**

Concurrency across ports is the composition root's job — expressed as threads or an adapter-internal concurrent call, with results entering the kernel as values in a defined order, so the kernel never observes interleaving.
Any port whose operations can be long-running exposes a cancel path that takes a handle minted when the operation started, and the adapter implements it as a real kill

GIVEN a dispatch that is cancelled
WHEN the adapter terminates the child
THEN the whole process group is killed and no descendant of the dispatch survives the call.

rows.statement: §3.3 gives `dispatch` a completed-value return and ADR-0076 makes every port method block the calling thread with the kernel never observing interleaving; a handle 'minted when the operation started' therefore cannot reach the kernel until `dispatch` returns, when cancel is moot, and the kernel has no clock (AC-001) with which to decide a deadline. Two competent implementers produce different traits: (A) `dispatch` blocks; `cancel` exists on the trait but is only ever invoked by the adapter's own timeout or by rk-cli's Ctrl-C path from another thread (the 'port operation' is vestigial for the kernel); (B) `dispatch` returns a `Handle` at once with a separate sync `wait(handle)`, so the composition root can cancel — contradicting 'surfaced as a completed value'. ADR-0076's 'any port whose operations can be long-running' also leaves open whether `Toolchain::build/test` and `DocsSite::build` carry `cancel`; §3.3 lists it on Harness only and no AC covers the others.
rows.why_before_step5: `rk-ports` (Step 7a) is the first crate whose signatures every later crate depends on; the trait shape chosen here is the one the fakes, AC-224's fixture and the composition root are written against.
rows.remediation: In §3.3 Port rules add a P10 fixing the call shape: name who may call `cancel` (composition root / CLI signal path, never the kernel), state that `dispatch` blocks to completion and that the adapter's declared timeout (AC-223) is the in-band cancel, and list which ports carry `cancel` (Harness only, or Harness+Toolchain+DocsSite with an AC each). Mirror the sentence in RUNBOOK 7a.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] All four anchors verbatim (design 266, 383; ADR-0076:54; AC 2890-2892). Searched design, AC, RUNBOOK and ADR-0076 for who invokes cancel (Ctrl-C/SIGINT/'calls cancel'): nothing names the caller; §3.8.2 (393) and ADR-0076:54 only say the handle is 'minted when the operation started'. §3.3 (266) gives `dispatch` a completed-value return; RUNBOOK 7c (2015-2017) has stream events 'surfaced as a completed value'. AC-223 defines the pack timeout but not that it drives cancel. The two-shape ambiguity is a fair [inferred] reading; the no-clock point (AC-001) is correct.
rows.material_reason: [measured] known-issues rows on cancel (ARCH-10.4-030, ARCH-10.x-T-021, ARCH-10.5-031, ADR-0076-FORB-78) all concern the Windows handle leak or dropped-future semantics, none the call shape or caller; NEW confirmed. rows.title: AC-224/AC-225 use POSIX process-group/fork/143 terms on a Windows programme; a tree-walk kill passes while missing F22-shaped survivors

*Verified by:* an integration test spawning a fixture that forks a grandchild, cancelling, then asserting no live PID in
the group; run on CI as a regression against F22's 12,000 s survivor.
WHEN the child exits 143 with no result message
a process-group kill of the spawned `claude -p` tree, with no descendant surviving the call
# taskkill /T /F the running process mid-graph, then:

rows.statement: The corpus runs on Windows (every RUNBOOK command is `cd D:/...`; the measured kill is `taskkill /T /F`), where there is no POSIX process group, no `fork`, and a terminated process does not exit 143. Two implementers read 'process-group kill' as (i) a Job Object with KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE and breakaway denied, or (ii) `taskkill /T /F` / a parent-PID tree walk. Only (i) reaps a `Start-Process`-detached descendant — the very shape F22 recorded as the 12,000 s survivor — while (ii) passes AC-224's fixture as worded (a detached process is by definition not 'in the group'). AC-225's 143 branch has no Windows instance, so its classifier test is unrunnable there as written.

rows.remediation: Name the Windows mechanism in AC-224 (Job Object, KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, no breakaway) and the POSIX one (setpgid + killpg); make the fixture's grandchild a detached/breakaway process so the tree-walk implementation fails; restate AC-225 per platform (Windows: the adapter's own TerminateProcess exit code, not 143).

Under (a) the fixture branch 'adding a sixth trait with no fake' only fails if the author also appends the trait to the list — the same manual act that would prompt writing the fake — so the number is asserted but discriminates nothing; the RUNBOOK's own warning names this failure yet its checkpoint only greps for the literal expression.

rows.title: reconcile() must both mutate nothing (AC-174) and delete stale clones (AC-193); two implementers build differently

anchors.quote: AND a stale clone found at entry is removed by `reconcile()` rather than reused.
THEN it completes and reports state and drift
AND it creates no commit, ref update, checkout, index write or stash.
| Reconcile is idempotent | **AC-175** — `reconcile(reconcile(w)) == reconcile(w)` over corpus histories, with an empty second drift set |

rows.statement: AC-193 makes directory deletion a side effect of reconcile(); §5.6 and AC-174 define reconcile() as a pure git→store read that 'mutates nothing in git' and must complete against a read-only git dir. Reading A: reconcile() reports the stale clone as drift and a separate entry-time step removes it; reading B: reconcile() itself calls the removal. Under B, a stale clone under a read-only mount makes AC-174 fail, and 'idempotent' (AC-175) acquires a filesystem precondition. AC-172's parenthetical also lists `status` among entries that 'can cause an action', which a second implementer would exclude from the reconcile_started enumeration.
rows.why_before_step5: Hygiene: decides where the clone-lifecycle code lives in rk-git and what AC-174's fixture must contain. No wrong thing gets built either way.
rows.remediation: Reword AC-193 to 'is reported by reconcile() as a stale-clone drift observation and removed by the entry's clone-lifecycle step before dispatch, never reused', keeping reconcile() side-effect-free; state in AC-172 whether `status` reconciles (it should, as a read of reconciled state, though it does not 'cause an action').
rows.truth_reason: [measured] Anchors verbatim; AC-193:2574 does say 'removed by reconcile()'. But AC-174 (:2364) enumerates five git mutations (commit, ref update, checkout, index write, stash) and §5.6:708 says 'mutates nothing in git' — deleting a disposable clone directory is none of the five, and the register names no clone location (grep: no AC gives a clone path), so the read-only-mount failure and the AC-175 'filesystem precondition' are speculative. What survives is a wording ambiguity: AC-193 attributes a filesystem side effect to a function §5.6 defines as a git→store read.

rows.title: Three vocabularies for the review stage weight (lenient/strict, deontic enum, numeric 0.2/1.0) with no stated mapping

anchors.quote: GIVEN a stage whose review weight is `0.2` (read-only advisory)
GIVEN any stage rigor weight in the enum
WHEN the stage's rigor weight is changed from lenient to strict
**The lenient default is the resolved weight when a stage sets none** (AC-298; ADR-0015 as renumbered by ADR-0020's deontic enum, `0.2 → optional`, `1.0 → mandatory`).

Stage rigor is a **deontic enum**: `forbidden < discouraged < optional < recommended < mandatory`, ordinal, never summed. Activities declare `min_rigor`. This supersedes the numeric weights in §4.2 and in D15 (review tiering).

rows.statement: AC-295/296/298 and ADR-0074 clause 5 parameterise the policy table by a 'stage rigor weight' with values lenient/strict; AC-303 and ADR-0020 make stage rigor a five-level deontic enum; AC-299 and AC-300 (both binding) write the weight as `0.2` and `1.0`, the numeric form ADR-0020 says 'is superseded'. Nowhere states whether lenient/strict is a second enum orthogonal to rigor or a projection of it (which of optional/recommended/mandatory is 'lenient'? is 'read-only' a third policy value or `optional`?). AC-296's proptest 'over every weight × every class' and AC-307's `stage_weight` event field therefore have no determined domain [documented].

rows.remediation: Amend the AC register: define `ReviewWeight = { ReadOnly, Lenient, Strict }` (or state the projection from the deontic enum explicitly, e.g. optional→ReadOnly, recommended→Lenient, mandatory→Strict) in one place, rewrite AC-299 and AC-300 in that vocabulary, and note in ADR-0020's successor that 'weight' in the review-gate sense is distinct from stage rigor if it is.
rows.truth_reason: All five anchors verbatim [measured]. expected_when_met`; `mutation-survived` iff a mutation was applied and the named suite stayed green;

rows.title: SM-086's target n≈500 cannot exclude the 0.6% comparator: 0/500 Wilson upper is 0.76%; n=637 is the smallest that works

anchors.quote: - **Target:** sustained below the comparator once n allows an interval that excludes it (n ≈500 blocks).
- **Kill:** a verified false-block rate whose Wilson **lower** bound exceeds 0.6% means the policy table, not the reviewer, is wrong — relax the weight before touching the card.

rows.statement: Wilson 95% for 0/500 is [0, 0.762%], which does not exclude 0.6%; the first n at which 0/n excludes it is 637 (0.5994%), and any observed false block pushes it far higher (1/700 → upper 0.80%) [measured, recomputed]. The target is therefore powerless at its own stated n — the defect class the corpus has already recorded four times elsewhere — and the register's rule that every quoted interval be computed here was not applied to the n.
rows.why_before_step5: Telemetry-only; no build impact. But SM-086 is the one measure the gate's calibration claim will rest on and its pass condition cannot be met at the n it names.
rows.remediation: Amend SM-086's target to 'n ≥ 640 adjudicated blocks at zero false blocks (Wilson upper < 0.6%), computed here; more if any false block is observed', or state the target as a bound rather than an exclusion.
rows.truth_reason: Both anchors verbatim [measured]. Recomputed Wilson 95% two-sided upper for 0/n = z²/(n+z²): 0/500 → 0.762%, 0/636 → 0.6004%, 0/637 → 0.5995%, 1/700 → 0.805% [measured]. The register's convention is two-sided (rule 3 at SM:18; SM:336 distinguishes two-sided from one-sided; SM-086's own 0/23 → 14.3% is two-sided). Caveat: a one-sided bound needs n ≈ 449, at which 'n ≈500' would be adequate, but the register nowhere adopts one-sided here. The '≈' does not rescue a 27% shortfall.

rows.title: AC-313/SM-087's $0 replay cannot take only recorded findings and still yield a non-empty block set under AC-287

anchors.quote: GIVEN one recorded `Findings` payload containing a `reproduced` finding, and the reviewed SHA
THEN the block set is identical on all 10 runs **and equals the expected non-empty set for that fixture**.
THEN the finding does not block, and the review outcome reports it as `Unverifiable`.
- **Sampling:** every release, on the pinned corpus; **$0** (recorded findings, no dispatch).

rows.statement: AC-313's GIVEN names a recorded payload and a SHA but no re-execution record; AC-287 says a `reproduced` finding with no re-execution record yields an empty block set; AC-313 then demands a non-empty block set on all ten runs. Either the replay re-executes the repro command ten times against the corpus fixture (not $0 in wall clock — F31 measured 250 s to >900 s per whole-suite run — and its determinism then rests on suites F31 Limit 7 records as carrying 54 and 62 baseline failures), or it replays a recorded re-execution record the GIVEN omits, in which case 'the machine half must not flip' tests only the pure policy function. Two implementers build different jobs testing different halves [documented].
rows.why_before_step5: AC-313 is the criterion the design says 'converts F29's 3-of-10 verdict flip from a correctness problem into a recall problem'; which half it actually pins must be decided before rk-kernel's replay job is written.
rows.remediation: Amend AC-313 to 'GIVEN one recorded Findings payload, its recorded re-execution record, and the reviewed SHA' and state that re-execution determinism is AC-288/AC-289's job; amend SM-087's instrument accordingly.
rows.truth_reason: Anchors verbatim [measured] but the dichotomy is not forced. AC-313:3916 'the confirm half' is ADR-0074's 'machine confirms' (classify + re-execute + policy), and the GIVEN supplies 'the reviewed SHA' so re-execution has a target. '$0' is glossed at AC-313:3918 and SM:652 as 'no model dispatch' — model cost, not wall clock. Under that reading AC-287 does not bite and the non-empty set is reachable. Residual: AC-313 never says in words that re-execution is inside the loop; determinism on the two non-green fixtures is an implementation risk, not a contradiction.
rows.material_reason: NEW (no known-issues row on AC-313/SM-087 beyond 'no baseline'). Priority corrected P2 → P3: with the natural reading available in the same lines, this is a wording clarification with no decision left open for the rk-kernel replay job.
rows.corrected_statement: AC-313 does not state whether the k=10 replay includes re-execution of `repro.command` against the reviewed SHA or replays a recorded re-execution record; the surrounding text ('confirm half', 'reviewed SHA', '$0 — no model dispatch') implies the former. Stating it explicitly, and noting that re-execution determinism on the two non-green fixtures is AC-288/289's concern, would close the reading.

rows.title: SM-089's landfill kill prescribes dropping advisory findings at source, which ADR-0082 forbids, without naming supersession

- Forbids expiring an advisory finding by age, run count, gate passage or stage advancement — retirement requires a re-review at a later tree or a recorded human dismissal.

rows.truth_reason: All three anchors verbatim [measured]. rows.title: AC-311 lets a human triage an advisory record 'into a quarantine'; ADR-0082 clause 4 makes that an error

anchors.quote: WHEN a human triages it into a backlog item, a quarantine, or a dismissal
4. **Advisory and `Quarantined` are disjoint.** `Quarantined { reason, by, until }` applies **only** to a finding the

rows.statement: AC-311 (human-gated, in force) enumerates three triage dispositions for a sink record, one of which — quarantine — ADR-0082 clause 4 and its forbids block ('Forbids applying `Quarantined` to a finding that was not computed as blocking') define as an error, not a no-op, because the override telemetry would record a suppression that never happened. *Verified by:* **routed to a human gate — not machine-decidable.** Reason: whether an advisory finding is worth a

- **Instrument:** the AC evidence ledger — `pinned` / (`pinned` + `unpinned` + `mutation-survived` + `not-feasible`) per item at stage exit.

rows.statement: AC-333 materialises an AC with no evidence as `unpinned`; AC-334 records a survived mutation as `mutation-survived`; AC-335, for the same 'green suite plus surviving ordering mutation' fixture, requires the AC be 'recorded `unpinned`'; AC-345 speaks of a separate 'evidence class' and 'pinned status'; SM-100's formula treats pinned/unpinned/mutation-survived/not-feasible as four sibling values of one field. rows.title: AC-344's generic block predicate contradicts AC-289 for mutation-survived findings, and the predicate is owned by two crates
rows.known_issue_match: none (AC-1.2-009 / AC-PROV-029 record only AC-344's advisory-sink dependency)

anchors.quote: THEN it blocks only if it fails on the candidate and passes on the reference
**AC-344** — `rk-kernel-verify` · evidence: §4.6 point 3 (proposal), brief §C.7 · decisions: ADR-0004, ADR-0019
THEN it blocks only if the suite is still green with the mutant applied.
**AC-289** — `rk-kernel` · evidence: F11 (S0.1: 15 mutants, 9 of 10 test-reachable killed, **1 survived**; test-reachable

rows.statement: AC-344 (rk-kernel-verify) is GIVEN 'a finding whose repro record names a command' — unscoped by class — and blocks 'only if it fails on the candidate and passes on the reference', routing everything else to the advisory sink. A `mutation-survived` finding's repro is 'apply mutant, run suite' and its defect signature is pass-on-both; under AC-344 it can never block, while AC-289 (rk-kernel) says it blocks exactly when 'the suite is still green with the mutant applied' and AC-340 says it blocks under the default weight. AC-344's four-cell truth table also duplicates AC-288's. The same block predicate is thus specified twice, in two crates, with incompatible results for one of the two evidence classes.
rows.why_before_step5: Step 7c builds both crates from this text. An engineer implementing rk-kernel-verify to AC-344 literally ships a verification gate whose own finding class (AC-340) never blocks.
rows.remediation: Scope AC-344's GIVEN to `reproduced`-class findings and cross-reference AC-288/AC-289 as the authority for the per-class flip rule (add a row to the §0.3 authority table), or delete AC-344's THEN and keep only its Unverifiable-to-advisory-sink clause. Decide which crate owns the block predicate and say so in both criteria.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] Anchors verbatim. But AC-284 (AC:3607-3609), forty lines above AC-289, partitions classes by repro shape: '`reproduced` iff a command ran ...; `mutation-survived` iff a mutation was applied and the named suite stayed green'. Under that table AC-344's GIVEN 'a finding whose repro record names a command' reads naturally as the `reproduced` class, so the 'mutation-survived can never block' contradiction requires reading the GIVEN wider than §9.2 defines it. What survives: AC-344 (rk-kernel-verify) restates AC-288's (rk-kernel) four-cell candidate x reference truth table and its Verified-by, in a second crate, with no cross-reference and no explicit class scope.
rows.material_reason: [measured] known-issues for AC-344: AC-1.2-009, AC-15.3-009, AC-PROV-029 record only the advisory-sink dependency; AC-288 has no row; no §0.3 authority row pairs AC-288 with AC-344. NEW confirmed for the duplicated-ownership defect. P2 sound: which crate owns the re-execution predicate is a record-correctness question with a one-line fix (scope AC-344's GIVEN, add a §0.3 row); no workstream is blocked.
rows.corrected_statement: AC-344 (rk-kernel-verify) duplicates AC-288's (rk-kernel) fail-candidate/pass-reference truth table and four-cell test in a second crate with no cross-reference, and its GIVEN is not explicitly scoped to `reproduced`-class findings; AC-284's decision table implies that scope, so the contradiction with AC-289 for `mutation-survived` findings is a plausible misreading rather than a stated one.

rows.title: AC-326/AC-329 whole-suite comparator has no bootstrap rule: the first affected run per toolchain has no total_test_count
rows.known_issue_match: none (ARCH-6.6-016 records the analogous p95 bootstrap for AC-330, which the corpus does state; this one it does not)

anchors.quote: whole-suite count for that toolchain
THEN it carries `basis`, `basis_reason`, `argv`, `selected_test_count`, `total_test_count`, `wall_secs`,
executed test count is not strictly less than the fixture's whole-suite count.
A run claiming `affected` whose executed count meets or exceeds the toolchain's last recorded whole-suite count is reclassified `whole-suite / selection-ineffective`

rows.statement: AC-326 reclassifies an `affected` run whose count is >= 'the most recent recorded whole-suite count for that toolchain'; AC-329 makes `total_test_count` a required field whose absence fails validation (and via AC-324 resolves to Err); AC-327's probe yields only a fixture's count, not the repo's. A filtered test run does not report the whole-suite total, so on the first run for a toolchain (or after any version bump) no whole-suite count exists. AC-330 states its equivalent bootstrap condition explicitly; AC-326/AC-329 do not. Two-implementer test: (a) force the first run per toolchain to `policy-forced` whole-suite to seed the count; (b) fill `total_test_count` from the run's own report, making selected == total and every `affected` run reclassify `selection-ineffective`; (c) treat a missing comparator as 'no reclassification', which is the exact fail-open shape AC-322 exists to forbid.

rows.remediation: Add a bootstrap clause to AC-326 (or a new criterion): with no recorded whole-suite count at the current version pin, an `affected` claim is reclassified `whole-suite / probe-unverified` (or the run is policy-forced whole-suite) and the resulting count seeds the comparator; state where `total_test_count` comes from on an `affected` run in AC-329.

Grep of AC/design/SM/RUNBOOK/ADR-0019 for 'whole-suite count', 'total_test_count', 'bootstrap', 'first run': no clause says what AC-326 does with no recorded count or where an affected run's `total_test_count` comes from.
