rows.title: AC-317 and AC-334 define two different per-AC mutation predicates (test-level x2 vs assertion-level x1); SM-094/SM-100 follow each
rows.known_issue_match: AC-0.3-032 (records the authority split 'AC-334 names the flip predicate; AC-317 is the harness', not that the two predicates differ); the §10 residual at AC:4450 records AC-334's derivation as unspecified

anchors.quote: THEN the named test fails under both mutations, and an AC whose test survives either mutation is refused at report time.
AND if the suite stays green the AC is recorded `mutation-survived`.
- **Target:** every AC in the fix and story lanes has a test that fails under both mutations.
**An AC is a claim about ONE ASSERTION, and Red→Green is evidenced at TEST granularity.**

rows.statement: AC-317 (§9.8) requires the named *test* to fail under two mutations (the implementation step 'removed, and inverted') and refuses at report time, with a 100% target in SM-094; AC-334 (§10.3) requires the named *assertion* to flip under 'the mutation derived from that AC's THEN clause' — one mutation — and SM-100 targets >=0.90 at stage exit with a human-gate residual. The design's headline (§6.5.3) is assertion granularity, which AC-317 does not require; 'inverted' is undefined for a step that is not an ordering or a boolean. Since AC-0.3-032 says AC-317 is 'the harness that produces' AC-334's class, the harness is specified with a different predicate, a different mutation count (2x wall clock against SM-094's own kill) and a different moment than the class it feeds.
rows.why_before_step5: Step 7c's mutation harness cannot satisfy both texts with one design; the wall-clock kill SM-094 predicts 'is very likely to fire' doubles under AC-317's two-mutation rule.
rows.remediation: Make AC-334 authoritative for the predicate (assertion flips under the THEN-derived mutation) and rewrite AC-317 as the harness-invocation criterion that calls it, dropping 'removed, and inverted' or defining the derivation once; align SM-094's instrument with AC-334.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] Anchors verbatim. AC-317 (AC:3956-3959): mutated '(removed, and inverted)', 'the named test fails under both mutations', refused 'at report time'; SM-094 (SM:701,703): ratio of ACs whose test fails under both, target every AC. AC-334 (AC:4146-4149): 'the mutation derived from that AC's THEN clause' (one), 'only if the named assertion flips', evaluated at stage exit; SM-100 target 0.90 with human-gate residual. §0.3 row 32 (AC:95) says 'AC-334 names the flip predicate ... AC-317 is the harness that produces it' — but the two criteria state different predicates (2 test-level mutations vs 1 assertion-level mutation), different moments and different targets. §10 residual (AC:4450) records only that AC-334's derivation is unspecified.
rows.material_reason: [measured] known-issues: AC-0.3-032 (AC:95) records the authority split as resolved by delegation; the §10 residual at AC:4450 records the derivation gap. Neither records that the two predicates differ or that SM-094/SM-100 follow different ones. SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed, citing AC-0.3-032. P2 sound: a harness can satisfy both by running a superset, so 7c is not blocked, but the record specifies one mechanism twice with incompatible parameters.

rows.title: Tick rules in decimal fractions: naive f64 passes every named vector yet mis-flags 80% of one-tick and 28/99 two-tick deltas

rows.statement: [measured, python 3.14 IEEE-754 doubles] `(i+1)/100 - i/100 <= 0.01` is false for 80 of 100 one-tick bases (e.g. 0.09 to 0.10 gives 0.010000000000000009), so an implementer who follows AC-372's 'at most 0.01' on f64 fails to flag most one-tick deltas; the runner's `delta < 0.02` (the F6 formulation) instead wrongly flags 28 of 99 two-tick deltas (e.g. 0.10 to 0.12 = 0.01999999999999999); AC-376's `>= 1.0 - m` misses the exact boundary for 7 of 58 margins (e.g. m=0.18: 1.0-0.18 = 0.8200000000000001 > 0.82). Every test vector the ACs name (0.100/0.110, 0.100/0.130, m=0.02) happens to sit where f64 works, and AC-374's ban on 'rescaling' discourages the integer-hundredths representation that fixes it.

rows.statement: AC-116's THEN clause describes a catalog whose family has a hole at r+1 and an engine that caps escalation at r 'rather than escalating into' the hole, on the same fixture ('a family with a hole at mandatory') that AC-048 says must fail load and AC-104 says must fail the check; ADR-0058's forbids block says such a family may not ship. AC-116:1530-1535 describes escalation `capped at r ... rather than escalating into` a hole on `a fixture family with a hole at mandatory`, the same fixture AC-104:1524 fails. rows.statement: Two different closed-output rules are in force for the same test. rows.why_before_step5: Step 5 writes this exact test. Implementer A ships AC-131's nesting lint plus AC-157's per-node branch count and allows a top-level `oneOf`; implementer B ships the RUNBOOK's grep and a per-type union-field count. Both believe they satisfied the acceptance set; A fails Checkpoint 5, B has no instrument for AC-131's 'nested-union fixture that must fail'. The set of legal Rust enum shapes differs between them.

AC-131 forbids only nesting; ADR-0084:64 and RUNBOOK:1741 forbid `oneOf` anywhere and are silent on `anyOf`; AC-157's Repaired note discloses abandoning '≤16 union fields' while RUNBOOK:1742 and ADR-0084 keep 'union fields per type' [measured]. rows.material_reason: known-issues search for 'oneOf|union branch|union field|AC-131|AC-157' returns only RB-GAP-006 (the grep exit-code shape), and the anomaly_pool has nothing; NEW stands. P2 is right: the stricter rule wins in practice, so Step 5 does not build the wrong thing, but the AC register, RUNBOOK and ADR disagree on what the snapshot test counts.
rows.corrected_statement: AC-131 and design §5.3 row 3 forbid nested unions; ADR-0084 and RUNBOOK 5.3 forbid `oneOf` at any node and are silent on `anyOf`. rows.title: No document says where a heading-anchored slice ends; AC-152's headings-in-prose test collides with AC-151's duplicate error

anchors.quote: GIVEN a document in which the target anchor occurs zero times, or more than once as a genuine heading
*Verified by:* an integration test writing arbitrary bytes (including markdown headings) into a prose section and
The one piece of markdown logic that survives is a **section locator** for the opaque prose fields — a heading-anchored slice, not a grammar — and it is tested as such.

rows.statement: The locator contract is stated only as 'a heading-anchored slice'. Nothing in the proposal, ADR-0005/0006, design §5.1 row 4, AC-149..AC-151 or SM-043 says (a) whether a section runs to the next heading of any level, of the same-or-higher level, or to a closing sentinel, or (b) whether a heading a human writes inside a prose section is a 'genuine heading'. AC-152 requires accepting arbitrary bytes including headings inside prose; AC-151 requires a named error when the anchor occurs 'more than once as a genuine heading' and forbids first-match. A human who pastes '## Acceptance criteria' into a notes section therefore either truncates their own section and duplicates an anchor (reading a) or is harmlessly accepted (reading b), and the decoy fixtures of AC-150 (fenced, indented, comment, blockquote) cover neither case. Two-implementer test: A ends sections at any heading and errors on the duplicate; B treats only the rendered template's own heading level as anchors and swallows everything below it as prose.
rows.why_before_step5: Step 6's rk-store locator is the one piece of markdown logic in the system and the thing SM-043 measures from first use with no baseline. The end-of-section rule determines which bytes are 'the prose field' and therefore what AC-149's byte range and AC-152's acceptance test even mean.
rows.remediation: Add one sentence to AC-149 (and design §5.1 row 4): 'An anchor is a heading at the template's declared level for that section; the slice runs from the line after the anchor to the next heading at that level or shallower, or end of file; headings deeper than the anchor level inside the slice are prose bytes and are not anchors.' Add an AC-150 decoy form for 'deeper heading inside the slice' and an AC-151 fixture for 'same-level duplicate inside a prose section'.
rows.truth_reason: All three anchors verbatim [measured]. AC-149..AC-151, proposal:268, ADR-0005:50 and ADR-0006 define the locator as a heading-anchored slice and never say where it ends: 'next heading', 'same level', 'heading level', 'sentinel', 'end of section' occur 0 times in the AC register, design, ADR-0005 and ADR-0006 [measured]. AC-152 requires accepting headings inside prose; AC-151 errors on 'more than once as a genuine heading' with no definition of genuine; AC-150's decoys cover neither a deeper heading inside a slice nor a same-level duplicate in prose [measured].
rows.material_reason: known-issues search for 'AC-151|AC-152|section locator|heading-anchored|genuine heading' returns only ADR-0005-FORB-49 (locator may not become a grammar) — the end-of-slice rule and the AC-151/AC-152 interaction are unrecorded; anomaly_pool has nothing. NEW stands. P2 is right: Step 6 can choose a rule, but AC-150's 'expected byte ranges' and AC-152's acceptance test cannot be authored identically by two implementers until one is stated.

rows.title: `Gwt` is undefined, migration cannot populate it without parsing, and AC-454's 'both fields absent' property is false by census

anchors.quote: | 1 | The AC type is `{ id, criterion: text, gwt: Option<Gwt>, verification: Option<text> }` — permissive by construction |

By the uncapped census the 19 specs hold 208 ACs, 77 with both and 29 lacking both [measured], so AC-454's property either fails or is trivially true depending on the unstated rule.

rows.title: Checkpoint 5's tests/snapshots path presumes a layout ADR-0083 forbids; the ADR layout puts insta snapshots elsewhere
rows.known_issue_match: RB-GAP-006 (RUNBOOK.md:1766, the checkpoint's false-pass reshaping; this is the false-fail the reshaping introduced)

anchors.quote: test -d crates/rk-types/tests/snapshots \
at most one integration-test binary per crate under test, structured as `tests/it/main.rs` with `mod` declarations for the cases — never one file per case.
cargo install cargo-insta --locked

rows.statement: insta stores snapshots in a `snapshots` directory beside the file containing the assertion. Under ADR-0083's mandated layout (tests/it/main.rs plus modules) they land in crates/rk-types/tests/it/snapshots/; as inline unit tests they land in src/snapshots/. Only a tests/<file>.rs layout, the one-file-per-test shape the ADR rejects, yields tests/snapshots/, so the test -d guard added to stop a false pass now fails deterministically for the conformant implementer and passes for the non-conformant one. The RUNBOOK also installs cargo-insta but never says to accept the initial snapshots; on a first run insta writes .snap.new and fails the assertion, so `cargo test --workspace # exit 0` cannot hold until `cargo insta accept` has run, which no line instructs.
rows.why_before_step5: Both halves are Checkpoint 5 lines; an implementer following the ADR hits two unexplained failures.
rows.remediation: Pin the location in the test (insta::Settings::set_snapshot_path) to a path the checkpoint names, or change the checkpoint to crates/rk-types/tests/it/snapshots; insert `cargo insta test -p rk-types --accept` with a review note before Checkpoint 5.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] Upgraded from the finder's inference: with insta 1.48.0 and the ADR-0083:74 layout (tests/it/main.rs + mod schema), the first `cargo test` exits 101 ('stored new snapshot ...tests/it/snapshots/it__schema__schema_snapshot.snap.new', assertion failed); tests/snapshots does not exist, so `test -d crates/rk-types/tests/snapshots` (RUNBOOK 1761) fails for the conformant layout. After accepting, exit 0 and the .snap lives at tests/it/snapshots/. RUNBOOK installs cargo-insta (1688) and mentions `cargo insta accept` only as a rubber-stamp hazard (1745); no line instructs the initial accept.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed against RB-GAP-006 (RUNBOOK.md:1766, the false-pass reshaping of the same line) and ADR-0084-NEG-89 (adr/0084:90, cargo insta accept as rubber-stamp) - neither records the false-fail for the ADR layout nor the missing initial accept. P2 sound: two deterministic Checkpoint 5 failures with a one-line explanation each; nothing built wrong.

rows.title: Step 5 owns both preconditions it marks 'unverifiable as specified' (AC-158 preserve_order, AC-121 two OS targets)
rows.known_issue_match: ARCH-5.11-009 / AC-UNVER-001 (record the two as unverified; do not record that Step 5 can settle both)

anchors.quote: half and `AC-158`'s property ordering are **unverifiable as specified** until CI fixes two OS targets and an
property order is not observable in the exported schema and this criterion is unverifiable — settle that in the runbook.
pull_request]`, a matrix with a Windows runner, `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` reading `rust-toolchain.toml`, and

rows.statement: AC-158 tells the runbook to settle order preservation; schemars 1.2.2 exposes `preserve_order = ["serde_json/preserve_order"]` in its feature list (measured in the local registry Cargo.toml), so one feature flag on rk-types' dependency makes property order observable and AC-158 checkable at Step 5. AC-121's two-OS precondition is decided by the CI matrix that 5.2 authors, which names only 'a Windows runner' (ADR-0084:60 says Windows is not optional, not Windows only). The runbook instead marks both unverified and moves on.
rows.why_before_step5: Both preconditions cost nothing at Step 5 and become retrofits later; marking a criterion unverified when the same step could verify it is the corpus's own anti-pattern ('do not let the phrase do the work').
rows.remediation: In RUNBOOK 5.3 specify schemars (and serde_json) with features = ["preserve_order"] and assert order in the snapshot test; in 5.2 name the matrix [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]; then strike the 'unverifiable' clause for AC-158 and AC-121's cross-OS half.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] schemars-1.2.2/Cargo.toml:49 `preserve_order = ["serde_json/preserve_order"]`. AC-158:1926-1927 says 'settle that in the runbook'; RUNBOOK 1777 instead says 'unverifiable as specified until CI fixes two OS targets and an order-preserving schema export - mark them unverified'. RUNBOOK 1671 names only 'a matrix with a Windows runner'; grep for ubuntu/linux/two OS in RUNBOOK and ADR-0083/0084 finds no second target named; ADR-0084:60 says Windows 'is not optional'. Both preconditions are decided by text Step 5.2/5.3 authors.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed: ARCH-5.11-009 (design:790) and AC-UNVER-001 (AC:1732) record the unverified state and call it 'a runbook decision'; neither records that the runbook did not make the decision it was delegated, nor that a schemars feature flag settles AC-158. P2 sound: a testability loose end, zero build consequence.

rows.title: Two more Checkpoint 5 lines cannot discriminate: grep -L 'workspace = true' and channel = "1.97
rows.known_issue_match: RB-GAP-006 (the checkpoint's false-pass audit covered the oneOf and ChangeSummary lines only)

anchors.quote: grep -L 'workspace = true' crates/*/Cargo.toml           # → empty: every member inherits lints
test -f rust-toolchain.toml && grep -q 'channel = "1.97' rust-toolchain.toml
cargo new --lib crates/rk-types

rows.statement: A member manifest containing only `edition.workspace = true` and no [lints] table satisfies grep -L 'workspace = true' (measured: empty output, exit 0), so the line cannot detect a missing lints table in any edition-inheriting crate. grep -q 'channel = "1.97' accepts a floating channel = "1.97", which ADR-0083:61/104 forbids (exact 1.NN.N only). Ordering also matters: cargo new run before the root manifest (the RUNBOOK's order) emits a literal edition = "2024" and no lints table, i.e. the policy restated rather than inherited; run after it, cargo 1.97.1 emits both edition.workspace = true and [lints] workspace = true (measured).
rows.why_before_step5: Cosmetic at Step 5 (one crate), but the same lines are reused as the 'every member' check through Steps 6-7 where hand-written adapter manifests appear.
rows.remediation: Use grep -L '^\[lints\]' crates/*/Cargo.toml and grep -q 'channel = "1.97.1"'; move 'write the root manifest' above cargo new in 5.1 so cargo emits the inherited fields itself.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] A member manifest with `edition.workspace = true` and no [lints] table: `grep -L 'workspace = true' crates/*/Cargo.toml` prints nothing, exit 0 (passes). `grep -q 'channel = "1.97'` accepts `channel = "1.97"`; ADR-0083:61 requires 'a concrete channel = "1.NN.N"'. cargo new 1.97.1 before the root exists emits literal `edition = "2024"` and no [lints]; after the root exists it emits `edition.workspace = true` and `[lints] workspace = true`. RUNBOOK 1613 runs cargo new before the root manifest at 1617+. Note the cargo-new-before-root manifest IS caught by grep -L (no 'workspace = true' at all); only the edition-inheriting case slips.
rows.material_reason: SHARPENS-KNOWN confirmed: RB-GAP-006 (RUNBOOK.md:1766) audited the checkpoint's oneOf and ChangeSummary lines only; ADR-0083-FORB-103 forbids `stable`, not a minor-version float. P3 sound: two non-discriminating checkpoint lines with concrete one-line fixes.

rows.title: gix pin location: ADR-0084 says the workspace dependency table, Checkpoint 6 greps the member manifest

grep -c 'gix = "=0.87.1"' crates/rk-git/Cargo.toml                       # → 1. EXACT pin, no caret

rows.statement: An implementer who follows ADR-0084 writes [workspace.dependencies] gix = "=0.87.1" in the root and gix.workspace = true in crates/rk-git/Cargo.toml; Checkpoint 6's grep then returns 0 and fails. An implementer who satisfies the checkpoint pins in the member manifest, outside the table the ADR names.

rows.remediation: Check the root: grep -c 'gix = "=0.87.1"' Cargo.toml -> 1 and grep -c 'gix.workspace = true' crates/rk-git/Cargo.toml -> 1.
rows.truth_reason: [measured] ADR-0084:58 verbatim 'in the workspace dependency table'; RUNBOOK 1850 verbatim greps crates/rk-git/Cargo.toml for the literal `gix = "=0.87.1"` expecting 1. RUNBOOK's other gix lines (1793, 1820) name the pin but not its location, so nothing reconciles the two; `gix.workspace = true` in the member returns 0 from grep -c and fails the checkpoint.

It runs on the pinned toolchain. `cargo audit` joins it under 0084. This is a floor, not a ceiling — it is specified as the minimum that must never be absent again.
